title: City's lord mayor-elect explains 'Hobart for Hobartians' slogan
text:
Veteran journalist and author Charles Wooley fronted the cameras this morning, for the first time since being elected late yesterday as Hobart's next lord mayor.

In the wide-ranging media conference, Mr Wooley raised several topics including the Israel election, statues, Julius Caesar, Donald Trump, King Charles and museums. He also avoided several questions.

"Let's get on together … I've been to some of the worst s***holes in the world. You are blessed to be here [in Hobart]," he said.

Mr Wooley's campaign slogan was "Hobart for Hobartians".

When asked what that meant, he said, "great question", before adding that the inspiration for it came from his travels in Barcelona in Spain, where he met that city's first female mayor.

"On the wall of her office she had 'Never forget for whom we run this city'," Mr Wooley said.

He was then asked what he thought about Hobart's council looking likely to only include one female councillor.

"Women didn't vote for women — it's extraordinary," he said.

As of 4:50pm yesterday, 50 per cent of the votes for Hobart councillor positions had been counted, with incumbent Louise Elliot the only female in the top nine.

Loading...

Mr Wooley was asked how he was going to address the division within the Hobart City Council.

"By being nice," he replied. "The last eight years of council have been vitriolic. It's been terrible and I think partly because we had a mayor who thought she was the boss.

"I'm not the boss. I represent the council to you, to the public, and I will represent you, the public, to the council."

In terms of his key policy ideas for the next four years of council, he said, "one way or another I'm going to cap rates".

"My own inclination is to give everybody a $200 rate cut and say, 'go and spend it in town'.

"My advisers tell me I can't do that, but we'll see," he said.

Mr Wooley said he supported council amalgamations and wanted the local government code of conduct legislation reviewed.

"Almost everyone in Tasmania is sleeping with a politician or knows someone who is. It's silly," he said

" I don't want to sound like Donald Trump, but let's make Hobart greater again. "

Chares Wooley says he will address the division that has been plaguing Hobart City Council. (ABC News: Greg Szabo)

Mr Wooley, who seemingly then forgot which side of the camera he was on — after many years of being the interviewer — then started asking the journalists questions.

"Let me ask some questions: do you own a house here? What is the budget of Hobart?"

Hobart Lord Mayor Anna Reynolds did not contest this election.

Several mayors not returned

Several mayors across the state ran for re-election but were unsuccessful.

Teeny Brumby has been Burnie's mayor since 2023, but lost out this time around to her deputy, Giovanna Simpson.

"Naturally, I'm very disappointed not to have been returned as mayor. I've given this role absolutely everything," she said in a statement.

"I've often felt like a special ops warrior, dropped behind enemy lines to clear the slate and rebuild the foundations! We inherited a city facing enormous financial and organisational challenges.

"For those of us who haven't been returned, I think we also need to acknowledge the increasingly hostile environment in which elections are being contested."

Teeny Brumby says she is disappointed she was not returned as mayor. (ABC News: Sandy Powell)

Clarence Mayor Brendan Blomeley was also not re-elected.

Newcomer Drew Jenner, who secured 51 per cent of the vote, will be the new mayor.

"I am proud of what we have achieved over this past term," Mr Blomeley said in a statement.

"I was humbled to receive the highest personal vote at this election, and I thank the community for their support and the opportunity to serve as their mayor."

Brendan Blomeley was unsuccessful in his bid to remain mayor of Clarence City Council. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Shane Pitt also lost out to Lindsay Newman on the West Coast, and Michelle Dracoulis has been replaced by Casey Farrell in the Derwent Valley.

"It's very disappointing … I absolutely put everything into this," Ms Dracoulis said.

title: Billions of dollars stolen in largest cryptocurrency hack in history
text:
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has suffered the largest hack in the sector's history, with attackers attempting to steal $US6.3 billion ($8.9 billion) in digital funds this morning.

The true scale of the theft is still unclear, with approximately $US3 billion ($4.2 billion) in funds currently frozen.

"This is definitely the largest [crypto hack] to date," said Nicholas Turnbull, a blockchain forensics expert and the director of Crypto Consulting Australia.

" You won't know [the full impact] until the dust all settles down. "

Binance confirmed in a statement to ABC News that it had been the victim of an attack, saying hackers may have gained access to a staff member's laptop.

"We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak," a company spokesperson said in a written statement.

Binance also said users should "rest assured that … [their] funds are completely safe".

Zhao Changpeng is the founder and CEO of Binance, which has moved to reassure its users following the hack. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

It added that the company, which is the world's largest crypto exchange, would cover all losses.

It appears the funds were moved from a number of "hot wallets" — internet connected wallets designed for high-speed everyday trading.

Thirty or 40 different tokens were affected, including Etherium, Bitcoin, and stablecoins such as USDT and USDC, according to crypto watchers.

RMIT economics professor Chris Berg, who specialises in blockchain technology, said not all the funds that attackers tried to steal will necessarily be successfully stolen.

"There are different layers of defence," he said. "Stablecoin providers can freeze those funds.

"[The hackers] have to withdraw it through an exchange somehow and that represents its own difficulty."

Australians facing spike in data breaches Australians should expect an increase in future data breaches as a result of critical software flaws that have forced major government websites, education platforms and web hosts to go offline.

Binance said it had temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals "while security checks are completed", and that an investigation was underway.

"We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice," it said.

While the precise losses were not yet known, it was clear the Binance hack was significantly larger than the next largest crypto theft on record, in February 2025, when the North Korean-linked Lazarus group stole approximately $US1.5 billion from another cryptocurrency exchange, ByBit.

Mr Turnbull said Lazarus Group was a likely focus for investigation in the Binance case too.

"This was a pretty sophisticated attack … you've got multiple angles coming on … so it's definitely a group," he said.

Professor Berg said the cryptocurrency sector has been plagued by cybersecurity incidents.

"It's one of the themes of the industry," he said.

There are concerns that improvements in hacker capabilities driven by AI, amplify that risk.

"[The Binance hack] may well be connected to what's been going on … around AI," Professor Berg said.

"For the last month or so, we've had a series of hacking incidents and discoveries of cybersecurity vulnerabilities … driven by frontier AI models.

"The hackers will definitely be using AI because everybody is using AI.

"The question is, was this only possible because of advances in AI?"

title: Hefty legal bill predicted in civil claim against ex-NRL star Jarryd Hayne
text:
A New South Wales Supreme Court justice says a civil rape claim against ex-NRL star Jarryd Hayne could become "an expensive piece of litigation" after mediation failed.

A woman who accused Mr Hayne, 38, of rape is seeking damages.

The woman had alleged the former Parramatta Eels player sexually assaulted her in her Newcastle home on the night of the 2018 NRL grand final.

Mr Hayne has always denied the allegations.

He faced three criminal trials and two appeal hearings over six years relating to the allegations, before his convictions were quashed on appeal in 2024.

In 2021, the woman, who accused him of rape, filed court proceedings in the NSW Supreme Court seeking damages.

Her claim hinges on the alleged injuries she suffered as a result, with a focus on alleged psychological injury.

'Very strongly contested'

During a status review hearing today, Justice Nicholas Chen was told by the parties a mediation session did not resolve the case.

Justice Chen said he was familiar with the case and suggested a second attempt at mediation, but did not make an order the parties to do so.

"I note the parties engaged in a mediation on September 4, 2026," he said.

"Is there any reason why I wouldn't order another mediation?

" I know enough about the matter to know it will be a very strongly contested and an expensive piece of litigation. "

Mr Hayne had a stellar NRL career before leaving the Eels to join the NFL, debuting in September 2015.

His three-year contract with the San Francisco 49ers was cut short after he was dropped from the team's main roster in November of that year.

He retired from the NFL in May 2016 and returned to the Eels, where he played until the end of the 2018 season.

Jarryd Hayne spent most of his NRL career playing for the Parramatta Eels. (AAP: Daniel Munoz)

In December 2025, his legal team sought to have the civil damages lawsuit against him dismissed, citing delays in the case.

At the time, his lawyer Michael Short asked for the case to be thrown out.

"I must say it is a long and well-publicised matter and there were criminal proceedings in relation to this matter," Mr Short said.

Ten days have been set aside in February 2028 for the matter to be heard.

title: 'Unqualified' assistance animals causing distress, handlers say
text:
People who rely on assistance dogs say untrained pets posing as service dogs are undermining the legitimacy of working animals.

Assistance animals are trained to help anyone from people with disabilities to people struggling with post-traumatic stress disorder.

But handlers in Western Australia's South West say unqualified dogs wearing the markings of service animals are causing distress.

Gary Crombie relies on his assistance dog, Levi, for his PTSD. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet )

In Bunbury, about 170 kilometres south of Perth, navy veteran Gary Crombie relies on his golden retriever, Levi, for his PTSD.

Mr Crombie said he had recently noticed what he called "fake assistance dogs" distracting Levi in public.

"There was this lady approaching me with her assistance dog," he said.

"When we got about five metres away from each other, her dog started to lunge and jump on its back legs, barking at Levi.

"The public behaviour in this dog was nowhere near meeting the standards."

'Anything could happen'

Mr Crombie said Levi had changed his life, helping him to leave the house while dealing with his PTSD.

"I was self medicating and drinking — the whole raft of things — but since I've had Levi, my whole life's changed," he said.

He said it was distressing for Levi to be distracted.

Gary Crombie says it is distressing when Levi is distracted by other animals. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet )

"[If] you get a dog all of a sudden attacking your dog in a public area where general dogs aren't allowed, it's quite disturbing," he said.

"When a dog is distracted, it's not paying attention to its owner and anything could happen to that owner."

WA Assistance and Therapy Dogs founding member Nigel Huckstep said he had also seen what appeared to be unqualified service animals in Busselton.

He said it could create prejudice against legitimate working animals.

"A properly trained dog will take 18 months to get to a standard where it can actually intervene with medical tasks," he said.

"Dogs that don't have training, that are effectively pets in jackets that behave poorly … you get the eye rolls when you're going with an assistance dog, particularly if you're able-looking — you have an invisible disability."

Different markers for dogs confusing

Accreditation for assistance dogs differs across Australia.

In WA, assistance dogs trained by prescribed organisations are recognised under legislation.

Assistance dog approvals issued in other Australian jurisdictions are also recognised and privately trained dogs can obtain public access rights if they satisfy approval requirements.

Assistance dog accreditation differs across Australian states and territories. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet )

Guide Dogs WA mobility instructor Katie Crawford said different markers could be confusing.

"Each organisation provides a uniform, so a legitimate jacket for an assistance dog or a harness for a guide dog," she said.

"That can then become quite confusing because organisations all have their own."

Ms Crawford said increased awareness around accreditation and service dogs was needed.

Katie Crawford says different markers for different organisations can make recognition difficult. (Supplied: Guide Dogs WA)

Change should not bring 'barriers'

University of Queensland law professor Paul Harpur said a national identification system could potentially provide benefit.

"The law deliberately focuses on whether the animal is appropriately trained to assist the person with disability, rather than simply whether it carries a particular badge, licence or vest," he said.

"Queensland has an example of a scheme that protects without being overly burdensome … I use a guide dog and I have a government-issued card.

Paul Harpur says any changes to regulations should consider people with disabilities. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

"That proves my right, protects shop owners or hotels from claims there is a dog on site, and gives everyone confidence."

But Mr Harpur said any regulatory change should not create additional barriers for people with disabilities.

"People with disabilities who genuinely rely on assistance dogs already face significant barriers to participation in society," he said.

" We should be tough on fraud and misrepresentation, but we must not create a system that treats every person with a disability as though they need to continually prove themselves. "

A WA Department of Local Government, Industry Regulation and Safety spokesperson said concerns about dogs' behaviour should be raised with the relevant local government.

"Assistance dog handlers who believe they have been unlawfully denied access may utilise the protections and complaint mechanisms available under the Disability Discrimination Act," the spokesperson said.

title: Schoolies-goers will pay to party on the beach for the first time
text:
For more than two decades, school-leavers celebrating on the Gold Coast have enjoyed a week's free access to their own dedicated safe space on the city's most iconic beach.

But this year, one night of celebrations will come with a $75 price tag.

On the second official night of schoolies celebrations this year, year 12 graduates will need to pay to enter the Schoolies Hub — a dedicated alcohol- and drug-free fenced entertainment precinct on Surfers Paradise beach.

The hub was introduced in 2003 to give high school graduates a safe space to celebrate with their peers.

Beach parties at the Schoolies Hub have been a major drawcard for the Gold Coast event. (Supplied: Schoolies GC)

Entry has traditionally been free for school-leavers wearing an official wristband.

However, the Queensland government has confirmed that, as part of a trial, it has allowed private operator Schoolies.com to host a ticketed music festival inside the hub on November 22.

A Department of Housing and Public Works spokesperson said the first-of-its-kind ticketed event would "diversify entertainment and inform planning for future years".

"This follows a roundtable discussion in June with the City of the Gold Coast, non-government-organisation partners and local businesses to continue and enhance the success of the Safer Schoolies Initiative," the spokesperson said.

This year's Schoolies Hub set-up, marked orange on the map. (Supplied: Queensland government)

School-leavers not wishing to pay the entry fee will still be able to access free activities on the Esplanade, including a Ferris wheel — another first for the event — which is being funded by the state government.

"With more than 20 per cent of Queensland's year 12 cohort continuing to choose the Gold Coast as their destination to celebrate the end of school, it is important to take a continuous-improvement approach to meet the changing needs of school leavers," the department spokesperson said.

Mayor against move

Gold Coast Mayor Tom Tate told the ABC he wasn't aware of the decision and did not support the move.

" Schoolies provide a positive economic impact for Surfers Paradise accommodation, paying high prices already, so I don't agree with charging them. "

Gold Coast Mayor Tom Tate says he strongly disagrees with charging schoolies. (ABC Gold Coast: Danielle Mahe)

School-leavers can pay up to $1,000 for seven nights of accommodation and must abide by strict rules, including bans on visitors to their hotel rooms.

Cr Tate said charging school-leavers extra fees risked damaging "goodwill" among young visitors, who could return to the city throughout their lives.

"The visiting schoolies are future customers for Surfers Paradise, returning for 21st birthdays, honeymoons and bringing their own family for holidays in the future," he said.

"This decision doesn't build goodwill."

Schoolies snub the glitter strip

School-leavers have been gathering on the Gold Coast to mark the end of their high school exams since the late-1970s.

However, attendance has declined in recent years, as graduates shun binge-drinking culture and choose overseas destinations such as Bali and Fiji.

Attendance at schoolies on the Gold Coast is on the decline. (ABC Gold Coast: Steve Keen)

Organisers estimate about 12,000 year 12 graduates celebrated schoolies on the Gold Coast in 2025, continuing a downward trend from almost 20,000 in 2022.

A Schoolies.com spokesperson said the ticketed event did not signal a move towards charging access to the Schoolies Hub but was instead part of an effort to help improve the overall Gold Coast schoolies experience.

"School-leavers will continue to enjoy free entertainment at the hub throughout the other six nights of schoolies week," the spokesperson said.

"We see this as an exciting opportunity to bring a major festival experience to the Surfers Paradise beachfront, creating something fresh and exciting that genuinely appeals to today's graduates, while retaining the safety and support that Gold Coast Schoolies is known for."

Schoolies week will run from November 21 to 27.

title: Australians stranded in Cambodia after cruise ship suspends operations
text:
A Queensland woman has handed over $63,500 from her superannuation for a dream retirement at sea — only to watch it unravel before she even stepped onboard.

Lisa McKay was weeks away from joining the luxury residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey when she discovered passengers had been forced off the vessel in Cambodia after it ran out of money.

The former teacher said she feared she would never see her money again after paying for a voyage she hoped would transform her retirement.

Fuel prices tank 'cruise for life' operator The US-based operator blames the ongoing fuel crisis for abruptly stranding hundreds of passengers in Cambodia.

"This was going to be my trip of a lifetime," Ms McKay said.

"I don't have that money to waste and lose. It's just been devastating, absolutely devastating."

On Tuesday, more than 200 passengers were told to pack their bags during a scheduled stop in the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville, with the company no longer able to cover the costs of operating the cruise.

The US ship set sail from Belfast in 2024 on a three-and-a-half year round-the-world voyage, promising residents visits to 425 destinations across 147 countries.

"Extraordinary increases in fuel costs have placed our current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement.

Brisbane passenger Rina Cavazza is among those left scrambling to find accommodation and make arrangements to leave Cambodia. (Supplied: Risa Cavazza)

Brisbane passenger Rina Cavazza is among those left scrambling to find accommodation and make arrangements to leave Cambodia after being forced off the ship.

Ms Cavazza, who paid $170,000 to live aboard the Odyssey, still had 18 months remaining on her voyage when passengers were told to disembark.

She is now staying in a local hotel and is making arrangements to return to Brisbane.

"It's been a sad time for many," Ms Cavazza said.

"We have had no word and no idea what is happening. I just know that this is our last day of access to the ship and I'll have one opportunity to go back and collect my belongings."

Questions about finances

The bulk of passengers onboard the Florida-based ship were from the US and Canada, according to the Cambodian government.

Some had sold their homes to pay hundreds of thousands of dollars for the years-long cruise, marketed as an alternative to retirement options.

Ms Cavazza said passengers were asked for funds to help pay for fuel, as far back as February and again, just before docking in Cambodia.

"Some people paid hundreds of thousands of dollars extra to help out with fuel," Ms Cavazza said.

Brisbane passenger Rina Cavazza's cabin. She has today to pack her things and leave the ship. (Supplied: Rina Cavazza)

Ms McKay, a former Brisbane school teacher, said she used her superannuation to pay for the trip via a direct bank transfer, and was due to board in Kuala Lumpur on November 15.

She said she had concerns about the company's finances after reading negative comments online and raised them with a booking agent, before paying.

In messages seen by the ABC, the booking agent said she "wouldn't be working for them if [she] thought they were in trouble" and that if the ship could no longer operate, the "company would arrange another ship".

Lisa McKay paid more than $63,000 for a dream cruise for her retirement. (Supplied: Lisa McKay)

"My chances of getting my money back [are] very, very slim," Ms McKay said.

"Travel insurance doesn't cover boutique ships."

Sign of things to come

In a statement, Villa Vie Residences said monthly fuel costs per cabin had averaged about $US1,800 but were now $US6,000 to $US8,000 in parts of Asia, due to the ongoing war in Iran.

"The company cannot simply pass increases of that scale on to residents, and the resulting shortfall has placed its current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure," it said.

It is not the only cruise company feeling the fuel crunch.

The world's largest cruise operator, Carnival Corporation, said higher fuel prices had added about $US150 million to its 2026 outlook.

The company recently announced it was halving its fleet in Australia next year.

Other major cruise operators such as Disney and Royal Caribbean no longer operate full-time in Australia.

Royal Caribbean said its fuel costs rose 27 per cent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, from $US279 million to $US355 million.

title: Cooling property market delivers $5 billion blow to Victorian budget
text:
Victoria's cooling property market has delivered a $5 billion blow to the state's budget forecasts less than a month before the state election.

An average of $1.3 billion a year is set to be shaved from the state's tax revenue over the four-year forecast period, according to a fiscal update handed down today.

"This is primarily driven by downgrades to land transfer duty and land tax, reflecting a decline in property market activity amid higher interest rates and other factors," the update said.

The government is still on track to deliver operating surpluses over the outlook period — but the expected average of $300 million a year is a significant reduction from the $1 billion forecast in the May budget.

And net debt will be slightly lower than previously forecast, owing to a lower-than-anticipated debt position in 2025-26.

Debt will climb to $197 billion in 2029-30, about $2 billion less than previously forecast.

But interest expense payments continues to eat into state coffers.

The fiscal update shows annual interest payments will be $8.9 billion this year — $24.3 million a day — rising to $11.9 billion in 2029-30, or $32.8 million a day.

"Victoria's finances are deteriorating and economic headwinds are accelerating," said Martin Codina, executive director of the non-partisan campaign group Amplify.

"Victoria urgently needs a plan to stop borrowing and pay down debt so that all Victorians can have confidence in the future," he said.

The books spell out nearly half a billion in savings since the last budget and also clarify that a clandestine myki surcharge uncovered by the auditor-general earlier this year, which Premier Ben Carroll said would abolished, will formally cease to exist on January 1.

Migration changes, material costs threatening state's outlook

The tax-reliant state is still expected to capture $9.2 billion in land transfer duty and $7.6 billion in property-related taxes in the current financial year.

The drop in property-related taxes was just one of several risks to Victoria's economic outlook that the report said "have increased in recent months and are elevated".

Falling prices in some parts of Melbourne's housing market is estimated to shrink stamp duty and land tax revenue. (774 ABC Melbourne: Simon Leo Brown)

Among them was recently announced federal changes to migration.

"If net overseas migration declines by more than currently expected, this could weigh on the longer-term economic outlook for the state through fewer consumers, lower education exports and a smaller pool of workers," the report said.

It also warned increased fuel and material costs, some linked to the prolonged conflict in the Middle East, could cause further cost headaches for Victoria's infrastructure projects.

Colin Brooks took on the role of Victorian treasurer in August this year. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Asked if his government took responsibility for the property market downturn, Treasurer Colin Brooks said the entire country had witnessed a similar decline, particularly in the eastern states.

"This is something that's impacting the whole country, driven by inflation, interest rates and also some changes in the federal budget settings as well," he said.

Mr Brooks said the $2.4 billion operating surplus recorded last financial year assured the state could responsibly deliver projects moving forward.

Auditor urges 'long-term' approach to budget repair

Melbourne has been at the forefront of a cooling property market, with declining auction clearance rates and subdued price growth linked to a slowdown in investment.

Mr Carroll has vowed to reverse increases to land tax unveiled in 2023 as part of a post-COVID budget repair plan if Labor is re-elected next month.

The tax, along with high interest rates and changing tenancy laws, have been credited with an exodus of property investors from Victoria.

In a separate report tabled today, the auditor-general's review of the Treasury's papers showed the state continued to record operating cash deficits, and called for more long-term approach to budget repair.

"The current fiscal strategy remains focused on short-term outcomes. While recent operating financial results have improved, fiscal cash deficits persist, debt remains relatively high, and long-term expenditure pressures continue to grow,'' the report saide

" Recent government initiatives do not go far enough to address the state's financial challenges or strengthen long-term financial resilience. "

Coalition backtracks on SRL vow as $1bn figure revealed

The Coalition has conceded that it will not pause construction on the contentious Suburban Rail Loop despite saying its policy is to "pause and review" the $34 billion project.

The government has confirmed pausing construction works, including tunnel boring, would cost at least $1 billion.

Jess Wilson's opposition has now said that it would not pause construction if elected on November 28.

Shadow Attorney-General James Newbury today qualified that work would only be paused if that did not breach existing contracts.

The Coalition had previously said workers would still be paid when work was stopped.

"The tools will be downed on anything that is not a breach of contract," he said, adding that workers would still be paid.

Works are already underway on the Suburban Rail Loop and the government has said pausing them would cost at least $1 billion. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)

Contracts totalling $15 billion have already been signed, and tunnelling is underway.

The cost of pausing and altogether cancelling the $35 billion SRL East has remained unclear throughout debate about the project's future, but frontbencher Anthony Carbines today said it would cost taxpayers $1 billion to "stop the project".

Mr Brooks, the treasurer, said the Coalition had now "effectively" adopted Labor's position.

"[It's] a complete backflip, they've effectively admitting they were lying to the Victorian people,'' he said.

Mr Carroll already cut $1 billion from the project, in part by cutting overpasses, walkways and car parks attached to planned stations.

He has also vowed to find another $1 billion through a "technical" review.

The first stage of a broader rail project spanning decades, SRL East is intended to link Cheltenham and Box Hill in Melbourne's east, but has been subject to speculation over whether its price tag and funding model are reliable.

title: Player prepares for World Cup after career reshaped by injury
text:
There are many things to prepare for when playing a game of rugby league. How to break a line, gain an edge or pick a way through a defence.

You don't prepare for one unfortunate tackle to alter the course of your life forever.

In 2020, at the age of 18, while playing for the Narellan Jets in south-west Sydney, Bryce Crane was on the wrong end of a tackle and suffered permanent nerve damage and paralysis of his right arm.

Yet, there was only one thing on his mind.

"You don't really quite understand how much something means to you until it is ripped away," Crane said.

"It's weird to think about but I didn't think about my life, I just thought that I lost the game that I loved growing up playing."

For the love of the game

Crane was told not to worry about the sport. Now, he is preparing for a home World Cup as Australia's Physical Disability Rugby League (PDRL) star fullback.

Australia will host New Zealand and England in the three-team round-robin tournament which runs from October 30 to November 8 in Sydney.

Crane (left) says it will mean a lot to once again represent Australia at the tournament. (Getty Images: Ashley Allen)

"It's really exciting to get into the World Cup; we have had a few camps with the squad, so we are getting around knowing each other," Crane said.

It will be his second PDRL World Cup after he starred for Australia in the inaugural edition in 2022.

Despite Australia failing to win a game, Crane's performances earned him a spot in the Rugby League World Cup Dream Team, which also contained players from the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments.

He was the only PDRL player in the team, and was named alongside fellow Australian internationals Josh Addo-Carr, Cameron Murray and Tarryn Aiken.

Bryce Crane was a stand-out for Australia at the 2022 World Cup. (Getty Images: Ashley Allen)

In the eyes of his teammates though, he does not just contribute to the team through his talismanic play.

Luke Vella, who is also an NRL assistant coach at the Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs, knows the hallmarks of a top-quality player.

"He is obviously very skilful and has a great ability to play the game, but he is very humble," Vella said.

"He is also very encouraging, there is times I know Bryce can make a break or make a tackle, but he puts others before himself quite often and encourages them and supports them along with their game."

Full circle moment

The final of the tournament will be held at the Sydney Football Stadium before one of the men's semifinals, the biggest stage the game has been played on so far.

Vella was injured at the ground while playing for the Bulldogs' under-20 side in 2014, and should Australia qualify for the decider, he will step onto that field for the first time in a playing role since then.

Luke Vella is part of the Australian PDRL team. (Supplied: Lainey Gaudron)

"It's funny, I haven't really thought about it too much to be honest," Vella said.

"Obviously the stadium got knocked down and rebuilt, it is a little bit different.

"I can't really describe what the emotions would be if we get there and I get the opportunity to play on the field again."

Vella's passion for the game quickly returned after his career-ending injury, and in 2019, he was named head coach of the Bulldogs' under-20s team, giving him a chance to push players to achieve dreams of making the NRL.

After coaching the team to the Jersey Flegg Cup in 2023, he earned his promotion to the first grade coaching ranks for the 2024 season, while balancing his return to playing.

He made his international debut for Australia against New Zealand in November 2024 in Auckland.

"When I got injured at 20, I fell back in love with it because it got taken away from me," Vella said.

"I love it because my thing for coaching is to develop players and help them achieve their goals, but then the competitive side, running around, throwing the ball around, a bit of contact too.

"All things rugby league, all come back to love."

For Crane and Vella, the pride in representing their country is palpable.

"At the end of the day, I'm not just representing myself, my family, my country, but I'm also representing people with all different types of disabilities," Crane said.

"I feel like that is a pretty cool thing to do."

This content was produced for the ABC's International Day of People with Disability coverage, which runs from November 19 to December 25, 2026.

The ABC is partnering with International Day of People with Disability to recognise the contributions and achievements of the 5.5 million Australians with disability.

title: Free hearing bus helping 2,000 kids faces closure as funding ends
text:
Jody Wright knows just how lucky he is to have a healthy teenager at home.

His son Eli had chronic middle ear problems as a child, and Mr Wright said a chance screening by a mobile hearing service in Dubbo, in western NSW, saved the boy's life.

Eli Wright has had three surgeries to remove a growth from his middle ear. (ABC Western Plains: Jen McCutcheon)

Eli was diagnosed with a cholesteatoma, a cyst that grows behind the eardrum in the middle ear, which can be fatal if left untreated.

"With his third operation … they cleaned the growth out, but it was millimetres from his brain," Mr Wright said.

"We thought we were going to lose him at times, but he's pulled through.

" If we didn't have the hearing bus, we'd have never known he had it. "

But the free service is at risk of closing.

The charity behind it has lost its main sponsor and needs to find up to $400,000 a year to keep running.

The Hear Our Heart Ear Bus Project offers free hearing tests in the western region. (ABC Western Plains: Jen McCutcheon)

Servicing the bush

The Hear Our Heart Ear Bus Project began in late 2011 as part of the Dubbo District Deaf Club.

The makeshift mobile children's ear clinic travels about 9,000 kilometres each year to more than 40 stops in Dubbo and western NSW, providing free hearing tests to pre-school and school-aged children.

Project director Donna Rees said in the past five years, "over 10,000 tests have been conducted, and half of those have been Aboriginal children within the region".

The tests have led to 310 children being referred to ear, nose and throat specialists, and 51 being fitted with a hearing device.

Previously, the allied health service had significant philanthropic backing through bequests.

The Hear Our Heart Ear Bus Project makes 40 stops a year around western NSW. (Supplied)

The Hall Foundation has been the principal sponsor since 2018, but made its last contribution in July.

The project is looking for new supporters to cover running costs of up to $400,000 a year or it risks closing by the middle of next year.

"The funding is desperately needed to continue funding the staff," Ms Rees said.

"We've literally got 10 fingers in 10 pies or more."

The Western NSW Local Health District declined to comment on the service.

Without the service, many families would have to travel to Dubbo for private screening.

"We'd never have been able to afford help, there's no way," Mr Wright said.

" It would be devastating; it would be a great loss to this community. "

The Hear Our Heart Ear Bus Project only has funding secured until mid-next year. (ABC Western Plains: Jen McCutcheon)

Closing the gap

The aim of the bus is to reduce rates of middle ear infection, or otitis media, and hearing loss among Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal children.

The condition is a major cause of long-term ear and hearing problems in Aboriginal children, with about 8,800 children affected in 2022-23, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

University of Newcastle professor and Worimi man Kelvin Kong is one of Australia's leading ear, nose and throat specialists.

He has spent his career improving access to culturally safe health care for Indigenous communities and said services like the ear bus were vital to help close the gap.

"Hearing loss is a developmental emergency," he said.

"It is so crucial that our children are hearing because if they're not hearing, they aren't learning.

"Hear Our Hearts do such an invaluable service to the community and they've been doing it for such a long time … they are incredible."

Kelvin Kong has a particular interest in treating ear diseases in Indigenous children. (Supplied)

In the case of the Wright family, it was not just Eli who received help.

"Sebby, my 7-year-old, he's got grommets through the bus and not only them two but my wife as well; she's got grommets and hearing aids from them," Mr Wright said.

"We probably would never have gotten it without the bus, we are very grateful."

Mr Wright said since the screenings, both Eli and Sebby were making inroads at school.

"They were having trouble in school, but now they are actually learning and they're coming home happy that they've gone to school so we're getting on with life now," he said.

Ms Rees said without the bus, there would be a lot of children sitting in school with hidden hearing loss undetected and undiagnosed and not meeting their potential with educational outcomes.

title: Dream shakes off scheduling controversy to force WNBA Finals decider
text:
Izzy Borlase's dream of winning a WNBA championship ring with Atlanta remains alive and kicking after the Australian rookie helped the Dream drag the finals series into a winner-takes-all decider against the Golden State Valkyries in San Francisco.

Game seven in San Francisco on Sunday (AEDT) should be a Halloween spine-tingler, with 22-year-old Borlase dreaming of joining 11 previous Australian winners of WNBA championships.

Opals ace Borlase was one of only seven players picked by Atlanta coach Karl Smesko as the Dream powered its way to an emphatic series-levelling 80-69 victory in front of a noisy near sellout crowd.

The Dream brushed aside the irritation and indignity of having to play the pivotal game six at lunchtime, rescheduled to accommodate a regular season home game for men's counterparts the Atlanta Hawks.

Izzy Borlase was used sparingly as the Dream leaned on the starting five. (Getty Images: Kevin C. Cox)

Increased interest in the Dream's finals run saw a number of games shifted to the home of the NBA's Hawks, which can accommodate 17,000 people, but game six was initially scheduled to be played at the Dream's regular-season home arena, with a 3,500-seat capacity.

After an outcry about the sixth game of the Hawks' 82-game regular season taking precedence over the Dream's push for their first title, the contest was moved to the bigger venue but forced into a 12:30pm (local time) slot to allow the Hawks to face the Cavaliers in prime time.

Borlase played very much a support role in her 12 minutes of court action as Atlanta's powerful starting line-up took control in an opening blitz and never looked back after holding a 17--point advantage at the end of the first quarter.

The Dream was sparked by Allisha Gray (23 points), Rhyne Howard (21) and another double-double from star Angel Reese, who had 14 rebounds and six assists to go with her 15 points.

Atlanta, shooting hot, only ever looked remotely rattled in the final quarter as the visitors, seeking to seal the win that would have brought them the title for the first time in just their second season, got to within eight points going into the final minute.

But there was no cause for alarm as Gray sank a three-pointer under pressure to get the home crowd roaring.

This marks the first time the WNBA Finals has gone to a decider since 2019, when the Washington Mystics beat the Connecticut Sun 3-2 in a best-of-five series.

This season marks the second time the championship has been decided in a best-of-seven format, with last year's victory by the Las Vegas Aces over the Phoenix Mercury coming via a 4-0 sweep.

Catholic parents in the Southern Highlands have been blindsided by a bishop’s decision to close their school in two years’ time. The move to shut down St Michael’s primary school in Mittagong, south of Sydney, comes against a backdrop of cost-cutting at Catholic schools across the state, but in this case, the local priest said the closure was due to declining enrolments with fewer families able to afford living in the area. St Michael’s at Mittagong will cease operations with students sent to another school in 2029. Google Earlier this year, more than a dozen northern beaches Catholic schools were told they would have to share a principal, while the Newcastle-Maitland diocese made over 50 school librarian jobs redundant. The sector’s overarching organisation, Catholic Schools NSW, has also been the subject of a corruption inquiry, which aired allegations that cash was used to branch stack right-wing Liberal Party factions.

Advertisement

Related Article Education Education boss to parents: Either share your principal, or pay $5000 extra a year On Thursday, families of the 180 students at St Michael’s Catholic Parish Primary School, Mittagong were told that in 2029 their school would be merged with St Thomas Aquinas Catholic Parish Primary School, Bowral, which is five kilometres away. Informing parents of the decision, the Bishop of Wollongong, Brian Mascord, branded the new arrangements “an amalgamation” of the two schools. The new school will be called Corpus Christi Catholic Parish Primary School and be located in the former St Thomas’ campus in Bowral. “I know this news may come as a shock and may bring uncertainty and concern for families,” he said in a letter on Thursday afternoon. “This is understandable and a testament to the great experience you and your family have had at St Michael’s or St Thomas Aquinas. At the same time, as Bishop, it is my responsibility to carefully consider and respond as best I can to the various needs of all people living in parishes within the diocese.”

Advertisement

He said the decision was made in response to a proposal from the Mittagong-Bowral parish, and factored in data, as well as consideration of the diverse needs of the people living in and around the parish. “At present, there are needs within the Mittagong-Bowral (and broader Southern Highlands) region that are going unmet,” he said. “While no decision has been made about how the site at Mittagong may be used from 2029, this change means the parish can explore options to meet broader community needs.” But that explanation made little sense to mother Jennifer Hogan, who chose St Michael’s for her children after moving to Mittagong from Sydney about a year ago.

Advertisement

One son is in kindergarten, and she previously had plans to enrol her two younger children at the school before the news. “The staff weren’t given any warning,” she said. “The whole thing feels gross: no consultation, no warning, and the information is convoluted.” “They’ve told us that a whole school is closing ... Is that because there is no other option? It doesn’t make sense – the Southern Highlands is booming. Why would you delete a whole school?” Corpus Christi Parish priest, Father Sean Cullen said on Friday the Bowral primary school had seen numbers decline steadily over a decade. Enrolment data shows they dropped from 380 a decade to 220 this year.

Advertisement

Related Article Education In selective schools, parental pressure is driving students to the psychologist’s office “And one of the reasons for that is [that] Bowral is an expensive place to live and people with young people can’t afford to live there,” he said. He said the decision would deliver “one vibrant school”. He said they considered moving the school to Mittagong but said the size of land of the Bowral primary school was bigger, but the deciding factor was the parish’s Bowral church was larger and could accommodate the entire school. So what is going to happen with the soon-to-be-empty school in Mittagong?

Advertisement

“We don’t know yet,” he said. “The Highlands has an older population, the demographics are quite elderly ... there could be a need for some care for the aged ... but we don’t know what’s happening with the site.” A Catholic Education Diocese of Wollongong spokesperson said neither the financial viability of either school, nor potential savings in education spending, played any role in the decision. “The amalgamation was not driven by cost reductions, but by a strategic response to a parish proposal following the 2021 merger of the Bowral and Mittagong parishes into Corpus Christi Catholic Parish. “The primary motivation is allowing the parish to address unmet pastoral and community needs in the Southern Highlands and maintain the ongoing viability of its ministries, while continuing to provide sustainable, high-quality Catholic education,” the spokesperson said.

Advertisement

The spokesperson said this week’s announcement marked the beginning of an in-depth consultation process where families, students, and staff would create the new school’s, identity, traditions, motto, and uniform. text:

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears ASX Runners of the Week: NGX Limited, RBR Group and Eden Innovations Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 30, 2026 — 3:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. This week’s Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is…NGX Limited.. It was another week when Wall Street demonstrated its extraordinary ability to make mountains of money disappear, artificial intelligence continued its expensive march towards world domination and Australian mortgage holders wondered whether the Melbourne Cup might come with an unwelcome interest rate surprise. Google parent Alphabet supplied the week’s biggest disappearing act, shedding a mind-bending US$500 billion (A$694B) in market value as investors took fright at the astronomical cost of the artificial intelligence revolution. Half a trillion dollars up in smoke in a single session. That’s enough to buy a fair chunk of the ASX, with change left over for a five-hour lunch and a 1961 Château Latour. Apparently, even Google’s “super” intelligence didn’t see that one coming! The sell-off followed disappointing earnings and concerns about whether the enormous sums being poured into AI infrastructure will eventually produce profits large enough to justify the expenditure.

Advertisement

The technology might be getting smarter, but investors are increasingly interested in whether the people paying for it know their times tables. Not that the AI gravy train showed much inclination to slow down. Anthropic, the outfit behind the Claude chatbot, filed for a blockbuster initial public offering that could reportedly raise as much as US$100 billion (A$143B) and value the business at somewhere between US$1.5 trillion (A$2.13T) and US$2 trillion (A$2.84T). Its prospectus revealed US$16.3B (A$23.2B) in first-half 2026 revenue, alongside an eye-watering US$80.7B (A$114.7B) net loss, much of it reflecting changes in the “accounting value” of its convertible financing instruments. Apparently, the solution to spending mountains of money developing artificial intelligence is to ask punters for an even bigger mountain of cash.

Advertisement

The proposed float could challenge Elon Musk’s SpaceX for the title of history’s biggest IPO, although the final price tag remains anyone’s guess. And while investors were trying to work out what the AI revolution was actually worth, the Middle East supplied another reminder that markets have more than technology valuations to worry about. Israel’s parliamentary election failed to deliver a decisive majority, leaving Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to face difficult coalition negotiations in a region rarely renowned for political tranquillity. With neither major bloc securing the 61 seats needed to govern, another political stalemate now looms over a region where tensions involving Iran and neighbouring countries continue to cast a dark shadow over energy markets. And with inflation already proving stubborn, the world’s central bankers could probably do without another geopolitical food-fight.

Advertisement

Back home, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was discovering that political life can be a nasty bunker shot, whether navigating the hazards of climate diplomacy in Fiji or the fallout from a round of golf in his own backyard. Senate estimates revealed a staggering $34.6 million in contracted commitments for the Fiji Pre-COP climate summit, including a significant spend on accommodation and event management for the three-day event. Officials expect the “indefensible” bill to be lower, but taxpayers could be forgiven for wondering whether saving the planet comes with too much Kava and complimentary cocktails. And just as Albo might have hoped to escape the financial rough, the Marrickville Golf Club affair popped up. A $6.05 million federal grant to the club in his electorate, where he had held an undeclared honorary membership before hastily declining the honour once it became public, drew fresh scrutiny. The PM was then forced to walk back claims the money was intended to fix sewage – read: bulldust – problems after the NSW Government pointed out it was already footing the bill for those works. Instead, the federal largesse was earmarked for clubhouse renovations and other improvements, presumably to make the place a little more befitting of its prime ministerial patron.

Advertisement

Between the Pacific spending debate and the golf club controversy, Albo has certainly had a week of hitting political one-irons. Unfortunately for the Prime Minister, there are no “mulligans” in the house of Reps. And speaking of household budgets, mortgage holders had good reason to reach for the absinthe bottle ahead of Tuesday’s Melbourne Cup. Fresh inflation figures showed annual headline inflation reaching 4.3 per cent in September, with underlying inflation still above the Reserve Bank’s comfort zone. The latest numbers had economists contemplating another interest-rate increase, potentially lifting the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85 per cent on the very day the nation stops to watch the ponies thunder down the Flemington straight. While punters study the form guide for a winner, the Reserve Bank could be saddling up another rate hike. And just like backing a horse that falls at the 400, this one looks capable of leaving everyone a little lighter in the pocket.

Advertisement

With technology stocks wobbling, geopolitical tensions simmering and Australia’s interest-rate outlook highly uncomfortable, the speculative end of the ASX had plenty of excuses to pull up lame. But a few small-cap hopefuls clearly missed the memo. This week’s podium belonged to African gold explorer NGX Limited, Mozambique LNG contractor RBR Group and concrete technology developer Eden Innovations, with all three producing gains that would have shareholders reaching for the French rather than the Disprin. NGX Ltd’s team during a recent due diligence visit showing the optimum terrain for exploration activities at one of its freshly acquired gold prospects in Namibia’s Damara gold belt. NGX LIMITED (ASX: NGX)

Advertisement

Up 92.9% (7c – 13.5c) Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is African gold hopeful NGX Limited, which nearly doubled its share price after unveiling an ambitious move into Namibia’s highly prospective Damara Gold Belt. The explorer charged from seven cents to 13.5 cents after securing agreements to acquire majority interests in seven Namibian gold exploration licences covering more than 1300 square kilometres, giving it a substantial foothold in one of southern Africa’s established gold provinces. Its proposed portfolio includes the Erongo and Otjikoto South gold projects, with Erongo sitting near WIA Gold’s Kokoseb deposit, which reportedly hosts a whopping 3.78 million ounces of the yellow metal. The ground covers geological structures associated with gold mineralisation across the Damara Gold Belt, while Otjikoto South lies near B2Gold’s established 1.95-million-ounce Otjikoto gold mine.

Advertisement

NGX can initially earn 51 per cent interests in the relevant project companies, with staged agreements allowing ownership to increase to as much as 85 per cent on most licences. Acquisition terms include initial consideration of up to US$545,000 (A$774,000) and further staged payments of up to US$2.46M (A$3.5M) over seven years, alongside exploration funding commitments and licence tenure conditions. Not content with gold alone, the company also secured rights over the 194-square-kilometre Karas copper project, just 10 kilometres east of Koryx Copper’s Haib deposit, home to 5.3 billion pounds of contained copper. Karas hosts known copper occurrences, including the historically worked Sperlingputs prospect, giving NGX another exploration string to its African bow. To help finance its ambitions, the company completed a $3.6 million placement bookbuild at six cents per share, with directors or their nominees committing $540,000, subject to shareholder approval.

Advertisement

The proceeds are slated to support exploration across Namibia and Malawi, with initial work at Erongo expected to include soil and calcrete sampling, field-based gold analysis and geological target generation. Several licence transactions remain subject to approvals and tenure conditions, so there’s still a fair bit of dirt to turn before NGX can claim to have struck the mother lode. But with its shares almost doubling, the market clearly reckons the Namibian treasure hunt is worth buying a ticket for. RBR GROUP LIMITED (ASX: RBR) Up 53.3% (1.5c – 2.3c)

Advertisement

Snagging silver was Mozambique-focused RBR Group, which surged 53.3 per cent after landing its first contract at the country’s giant LNG developments since force majeure restrictions were lifted. The company’s Projectos Dinamicos subsidiary landed a US$2M (A$2.84M) subcontract to manufacture and deliver 32 accommodation modules and associated facilities for at least 100 workers at ExxonMobil’s Rovuma LNG project in northern Mozambique. The contract forms part of a broader US$7M (A$9.95M) accommodation package and represents the first stage of a development ultimately intended to house about 700 personnel. Manufacturing is scheduled to begin in early November, with delivery targeted for late January 2027. For RBR, which has spent years positioning itself to provide workforce services, training and infrastructure support to Mozambique’s gas industry, the deal represents a potentially important commercial breakthrough.

Advertisement

The country’s LNG developments have endured prolonged disruption from security concerns and project delays, leaving contractors waiting for major construction activity to resume. Now RBR has an actual contract to show for its persistence. And while A$2.84M might barely cover the morning coffee bill on a multibillion-dollar LNG development, it looks like a solid starting point for a small company establishing itself in the supply chain. RBR says Projectos Dinamicos and its Futuro Skills business are pursuing tender opportunities with a combined potential value of approximately US$100M (A$142M). Those opportunities are not yet secured revenue, but they offer a glimpse of the prize RBR hopes to chase as Mozambique’s gas sector gathers momentum.

Advertisement

Successful delivery of the accommodation modules could strengthen the company’s credentials for future work, although additional contracts are far from guaranteed. After years of waiting for Mozambique’s LNG juggernaut to get moving, RBR has finally managed to get a foot in the door. Now comes the hard part — making sure the door stays open and the contracts keep rolling in. Proposed 16-story Aliyah apartments in Denver, Colorado, USA requiring 18,350 cubic metres of concrete. Eden Innovation’s EdenCrete Pz7 will be used in multiple types of concrete in the project. EDEN INNOVATIONS LIMITED (ASX: EDE) Up 44% (5c – 7.2c)

Advertisement

Taking the final podium spot was concrete technology hopeful Eden Innovations, proving that even an industry built around watching things harden can produce lively share-price action. Eden’s shares climbed 44 per cent after the company delivered updates on its expanding US commercial pipeline and followed up with another order for its EdenCrete concrete admixture technology. EdenCrete products are designed to improve concrete performance, targeting strength, durability and resistance to deterioration. It is not technology likely to set hearts racing at a dinner party; however, in a global construction industry consuming enormous volumes of concrete, even modest performance improvements can create substantial commercial opportunities. Eden began the week outlining progress across its United States project pipeline, where it’s been quietly building acceptance of its technology among construction companies and infrastructure customers.

Advertisement

Then came a more tangible development from South America. On Thursday, the company announced a further A$475,000 order for EdenCrete Pz7, adding another commercial sale to its international ambitions. For a technology developer attempting to persuade a traditionally conservative industry to embrace new materials, repeat orders can carry considerable weight. The challenge is not simply proving a product works in a laboratory, but convincing customers to use it on real projects and then come back for more. Eden’s latest South American order suggests good progress, although sustained sales growth is still needed to demonstrate the technology’s long-term commercial potential.

Advertisement

And with construction rarely accused of moving at lightning speed, product approvals, testing requirements and customer adoption can influence how quickly opportunities become revenue. Nevertheless, investors clearly liked the combination of an expanding project pipeline and another “set in concrete” order. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Australia’s staging of the Rugby League World Cup has been a raging success on the surface, drawing strong crowds and television ratings and already featuring an epic showdown between the Kangaroos and New Zealand. But behind the scenes, there is unrest about a landscape of haves and have-nots in the international game rearing its head. Loading Officials from some of the cash-strapped nations are disgruntled about having to fork out tens of thousands of dollars for corporate boxes at their own games to the Australian Rugby League Commission, the tournament organiser. ARL Commission executive chairman Peter V’landys has hosted guests in plush facilities at the Kangaroos’ two matches to date, against the Kiwis at Allianz Stadium and against Fiji at Brisbane’s Suncorp Stadium last Sunday.

Advertisement

But governing bodies from other nations have been forced to dig into limited funds to pay for corporate suites to entertain their VIPs and sponsors when their teams are playing, rather than having them provided by the World Cup hosts. On Friday, V’landys defended the planning for the tournament, pointing to the funds provided to competing nations. According to sources with knowledge of the issue, speaking on the condition of anonymity, Papua New Guinea officials even considered abandoning hosting games during the World Cup if boxes were not made available. Australia and New Zealand opened the tournament at Allianz Stadium before a crowd of 41,255. Getty Images There was heightened sensitivity over that situation given the Australian government is ploughing $600 million into the code to bankroll the incoming PNG Chiefs and the expansion of rugby league in the Pacific and ward off the influence of China in the region. In the end, the policy was relaxed for PNG. The men’s national team, the Kumuls, and women’s side, the Orchids, have since played two World Cup games each in Port Moresby.

Advertisement

Other nations, however, have had to stump up as much as $30,000 to the ARL Commission for corporate facilities, a departure from the Pacific Championships where boxes and suites have been supplied to participating countries. “It’s been an absolute joke,” one national official said. The PNG women’s team celebrates scoring a try against France in Port Moresby. Competing nations are also unhappy about the gulf between the treatment of their players and the Australian team. There is a long-standing disparity in player remuneration – members of Kevin Walters’ squad will receive $40,000 for the World Cup while players from other countries will earn only $850 per game. The Australian fees are dictated by the Rugby League Players’ Association’s collective bargaining agreement with the ARL Commission.

Advertisement

But officials at the World Cup are also annoyed at their players having to share twin rooms at rundown hotels and at times sleep in single beds while the Australians are put up in their own rooms at top-end lodgings. V’landys, who has been on a trip to China this week to source equipment for his planned “NRL Land” entertainment centre and meet stadium representatives in Hong Kong, explained the role of the World Cup hosts on Friday. Fiji fans cheer during the Bati’s game against Australia in Brisbane last weekend. Getty Images “Every nation executes a participation agreement. Accordingly, we pay each nation a participation payment,” he said. “In addition, we make payments to the players, pay for flights, accommodation, travel and meals for 32 players and officials [per team]. We also provide 112 complimentary admission tickets [and] prize money of $475,000 each for the men’s and women’s [World Cups]. We invite travelling administrators into [the] official ARLC function.

Advertisement

“As you can see, we cover nearly all costs and pay them to participate. They signed an agreement and knew of the terms. [It’s] disappointing they cherry-pick; as you can see, they receive a very good deal.” V’landys said the pre-tournament complication with PNG emerged because administrators there mistakenly believed they were a host nation and had committed to providing boxes they weren’t entitled to. The Tongan team trains before their blockbuster group game against Samoa at CommBank Stadium on Sunday. Kate Geraghty “We helped them out by giving up the ARLC box and other boxes to cover their mistake,” he said. “We acted in good faith as they made a mistake and were never threatened about them pulling out.” Another source of displeasure among some officials is suggestions that Australia and New Zealand will get first choice of hotels for the semi-finals in Sydney and Newcastle despite the fact the Kiwis will finish second in Pool A in the men’s tournament following a 24-22 defeat to the Kangaroos on October 15.

Advertisement

The reward for winning Pool B, meanwhile, is a six-day turnaround in a secondary hotel in Newcastle. Related Article Exclusive

This is what shocked him in jail National teams are wary about airing their frustrations publicly, considering the importance of Australia to international competition and the comparative commercial might of the ARL Commission, which owns the NRL. However, the experience of this World Cup could shape decision-making regarding the next one. Sources say the International Rugby League will no longer sell rights to the World Cup to a host country or countries and instead plans to run future editions itself, possibly in partnership with the ARL Commission.

Advertisement

Under one scenario to be discussed at an IRL board meeting next week, the ARL Commission would jointly underwrite the 2030 World Cup despite Australia not physically hosting it. The location of the tournament is set to be announced next month. Recent developments have helped convince the international federation, on whose board V’landys sits, to go in the new direction. The IRL is in dispute with England’s Rugby Football League over $800,000 in allegedly outstanding payments from the 2022 World Cup, while the original host of this year’s tournament, France, withdrew for financial reasons, leading Australia to step in.

I like the fact that we’ve given the younger guys a chance to grow, without the experience sitting on their shoulder. “We always said we’d lean back into the experience when we wanted to, but he’s coming in to predominantly drive that second five-eighth position, at 12. Wallabies coach Les Kiss fronts media on Friday. Oscar Colman “He can flex into 15 and 10 in our sessions and how we build our game going forward, so we just need him in that space, and he’ll bring his experience in his way.” Ahead of matches against England, Scotland and Wales Kiss is focused on giving the squad’s playmakers of Gordon, Ben Donaldson and Declan Meredith a chance to “own” their position and drive the team.

“I’m actually empowering them to say go for it and do it and have permission to just lead this team,” Kiss said. Kiss will use training in London next week to determine Gordon’s fitness to face England, after the five-eighth was involved in sessions this week in Sydney. Carter Gordon will be assessed further in London before a decision is made on his fitness. Getty Images “We just need to get a feel for it [Gordon’s fitness] when we hit the ground, particularly on Monday and the Tuesday session; we’ll just be a little bit more informed where we take that,” Kiss said. “I would say the Tuesday session might just give us a few clues where we go [at five-eighth]. We may not know our full team. Usually, I try to name the team that day.”

Advertisement

The Wallabies coach was more positive about the fitness of breakaway Tom Hooper, saying scans “have cleared everything” after Hooper suffered a shoulder injury while playing for Exeter against Bristol. There were initial fears Hooper could have aggravated the shoulder injury he sustained in the Test against Ireland in July, but Kiss said he will “join the camp in a good way” with full movement returning. Dylan Pietsch will have to bide his team after missing the Wallabies Spring tour. Getty Images A notable omission from the Wallabies’ squad was in-form winger Dylan Pietsch, who scored two tries for Australia A against the USA last Sunday in Nashville. Kiss said the Western Force winger had been considered after recovering from a foot injury, but he also wanted to provide more cover for Tom Wright at fullback with James Ramm. Kiss also confirmed France-based Tom Banks was discussed by the coaching staff.

Related Article Wallabies James Ramm dreamed of going to the Olympics as a gymnast. Now he’s chasing a Wallabies debut “One thing that has happened when an injury happens, it’s becoming really difficult to move the person that comes in, and they’ve been performing either in training or playing,” he said. “And how do we get those blokes back in? It’s more difficult to get back in, and that’s what it should be – more competitive. Now, you know, Dylan’s sitting right here in that selection frame for sure... “We just wanted to get another 15 in play and look at another 15, so we looked at what our options there with Jock [Campbell] moving to Japan and in this period just not available. “We looked at [Western Force’s] Mac Grealy, who we know enough about, [Montpellier’s] Tom Banks we had a look at, and obviously James Ramm.”

England are ranked fifth in the world and have lost three of their past five games. Kiss said England were moving to a more attack-based game, giving the Wallabies a significant challenge as a tour opener at Twickenham. “There’s no better place in rugby in a lot of ways [than Twickenham] in terms of those wonderful battles between Australia and England,” he said. “The game that they’re playing, it certainly has the tenets of set piece and kicking are central, but you can see ... they’re going to have an attacking edge to them as well. “So there are real challenges that we know that are ahead of us, but that’s what we need. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has awarded three ministers additional staffers worth a total of $550,000, as crossbench MPs accuse him of failing to play fair over his power to decide opponents’ staffing levels. Defence Minister Richard Marles, Emergency Management Minister Kristy McBain and Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino each hired an additional staff member between May and October, while allocations for the Greens, One Nation and independents remained flat. Defence Minister Richard Marles (left) and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese (right). Dominic Lorrimer The government now employs 433 adviser-level staff among their 30 ministers, with a maximum total remuneration for the cohort of a little more than $96 million. By comparison, the shadow ministry currently employs 92 advisers on a maximum total remuneration of just above $19 million. The prime minister’s sole discretion to set additional staffing allocations for both his ministers and his opponents has come under increased scrutiny with both One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and independent senator Fatima Payman heaping pressure on Albanese to hand the power to an independent body.

Advertisement

On Thursday, this masthead revealed that One Nation MP David Farley had rejected an unsolicited offer from Albanese to employ an additional staffer, with a $200,000 salary package, over concerns the prime minister was seeking to influence the lower-house politician. It follows similar revelations in this masthead that Albanese wrote a letter guaranteeing 15 staff to the Greens three days before the party teamed up with Labor to reject an inquiry into his power to allocate staff; allowed Senator Tammy Tyrrell to retain additional staff when she joined Labor in May; and offered then-opposition leader Sussan Ley additional staff for support of the government’s attempt to change freedom of information laws. Albanese defended his provision of staffing on Thursday, saying he had increased the staffing allocation to all federal MPs during his time as prime minister. While all federal MPs can now employ five electorate officers, up from four, Albanese has complete discretion over how many higher-paid advisers each MP gets. Electorate officers have a base salary of up to $102,681, while adviser-level staff for ministers can earn up to $317,152, and $167,530 for all other MPs.

Advertisement

The latest data, accurate as of October 1, found Marles and Mulino had each hired one “adviser 3” grade staffer with a base salary up to $167,530. McBain hired an “adviser 2″ grade staffer with a base salary up to $113,521. All three staffers can also collect $35,387 in allowances. Marles now has 20 advisers, McBain has eight and Mulino has seven. Related Article Exclusive

One Nation Albanese offered One Nation MP an extra staffer. Hanson says it’s an attempt at undue influence The offices of Albanese, Marles, Mulino and McBain were all contacted for comment regarding the responsibilities of the additional staff and the specific pay grade determinations. None responded prior to publication. Northern Territory MP Luke Gosling appears to have lost two staffers when he stood aside from a special envoy role after being charged with breaching bail conditions while awaiting a court date for an alleged assault. Gosling’s breach of bail charge has since been dropped. He is facing two charges of assaulting the Northern Territory administrator, which he denies. Payman is the only independent in the parliament who has no advisers. The senator believes Albanese is punishing her for defecting from the Labor Party during the last term of parliament.

Advertisement

Integrity experts and crossbench MPs have repeatedly called for the power to be handed to an independent body over fears the prime minister is “weaponising” his power. MPs’ salaries are set by the independent Remuneration Tribunal, a body that has been floated as a more appropriate way to decide staffing allowances. More than 18,000 passengers boarded driverless trains at stations along the final stage of Sydney’s $30 billion M1 metro line for the first time on Friday morning, creating a carnival atmosphere and ending more than two years of major disruptions. In a historic milestone for the mega project, the opening of the 13-kilometre section between Bankstown and Sydenham completes the 66-kilometre M1 line which has been built in three stages over more than a decade and now connects the south-west to the north-west via the central city. People gathered well before 4am at Bankstown for the opening of the Southwest section of the M1 metro line. Audrey Richardson The first train service was jam-packed with rail enthusiasts and residents from Sydney’s south-west. Audrey Richardson The 18,000 trips taken up until 10am from the 10 stations along the Southwest section on Friday took total patronage along the entire M1 line to 92,000 journeys during the morning period.

Advertisement

Premier Chris Minns paid tribute to the project team, engineers and others who were responsible for turning a 130-year-old heavy rail line in the south-west into a 21st-century metro railway. “It was incredibly difficult. It was expensive. It did take time. I’m so pleased they did it, however,” he said. “We’ve seen a big boom in suburbs along the metro line, wherever it’s been built, and I expect the same thing to happen on this Canterbury-Bankstown corridor.” More than 1000 people lined up behind a belt barrier on the platform at Bankstown station before cramming on board the first metro service. Audrey Richardson Melburnian Ash Williamson (left) and friend Steven McPhearson on the first southbound train after earlier catching the inaugural service from Bankstown. Audrey Richardson About 1200 people turned up to catch the first service, which pulled out of Bankstown station on time at 4.31am to loud cheers.

Earlier, Bankstown Labor MP Jihad Dib cut the ribbon for the Southwest Metro project at the entrance to the station, joined by fellow MPs Jo Haylen and Sophie Cotsis about 40 minutes before the first train departed. The extended metro line operated smoothly during the morning peak, which was its first major test. Summer Hill MP Jo Haylen and Premier Chris Minns board a metro train at Sydenham for a ride to Dulwich Hill on Friday morning. Sitthixay Ditthavong Passengers alight after riding the first southbound M1 train service which arrived at Bankstown before dawn. Sitthixay Ditthavong Unsurprisingly, Bankstown station recorded the highest number of boardings on the new Southwest section, as more than 3000 passengers used it up to 10am, followed by Campsie.

Advertisement

The opening of the final stretch was a relief for commuters who have endured trips on pink replacement buses for the past two years while the T3 heavy rail line was converted to handle fully autonomous metro trains. At Dulwich Hill station, resident Ylana Magni said the community mood was celebratory after the start of metro services. “I think it’s going to be more popular than we realise,” she said. Nick Plummer and Patrick, aged 7, catch the first service. Sitthixay Ditthavong Metro trains pass through Hurlstone Park station on Friday. Sitthixay Ditthavong Will Randall, who studies engineering at the University of NSW, said the metro line would shave about 15 minutes off his morning commute from Dulwich Hill. “[It has been a] long time coming, but [I’m] thankful that it’s here. It’s going to make the commute a lot quicker,” he said.

Transport Minister John Graham, who was on board the first service, said south-west residents were relieved the metro line had opened. “It was a relief as the train took off this morning,” he said. He acknowledged the drivers who had operated the pink buses over the last two years, although conceded that the community will not miss the replacement services. Train lover Sparsh Singla shows off his badge haul. Sitthixay Ditthavong “I know everyone’s happy to be off the pink buses … [but the drivers have] been really important to this community over the last couple of years,” he said. The pink replacement buses will continue running along the south-west corridor over the weekend as a back-up before they are removed, which should reduce congestion on local roads.

Like the rest of the M1 line, trains run every four minutes on the Southwest section during weekday peak hours, every five minutes between 10am and 3pm, and every 10 minutes in the evenings and on weekends. Related Article Sydney Metro Twists and turns in Sydney’s most difficult metro train project However, they have been boosted to one every seven minutes this weekend to accommodate greater interest. While the fully completed M1 metro line is popular, Minns reiterated that the driverless rail projects were “very expensive” to build. “They transform cities, but [you] shouldn’t forget the price tag. They’re incredibly expensive, and we will build metros when we can afford to build them,” he said.

He disclosed on Monday that the final section of the M1 metro line cost $10 billion. The government has not previously broken out the cost of converting the T3 heavy rail line to metro train standards, referring only to the combined bill for the city and Southwest sections of nearly $23 billion. text:

CultureBooksReview Rage, depression, despair: Why is PMDD still so poorly understood? Heidi Maier October 30, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
