Gender difference is intimately stitched into the fabric of humanity, and at every stage in its long history, medicine has absorbed and enforced socially constructed divisions and assumptions. These divisions have traditionally ascribed power and dominance to men. As modern scientific medicine evolved into a discipline, institution and profession, it flourished within these dynamics. Women were marked by their anatomical difference from men, and medically defined as defective, deficient and deviant. But women also possessed an organ of the highest biological – and social – value: the uterus. Possession of this organ defined the purpose of women: to bear and raise children. Being biologically female defined and constrained what it meant to be a woman. And being a woman was conflated with, and reduced to, “the female sex”. Medicine validated these social determinants by constructing the myth that woman was her biology, both physically and psychologically, and for centuries, women’s illnesses and diseases were consistently related back to the “secrets” and “curiosities” of their reproductive organs, menstruation, pregnancy and childbirth. Writer Laura Elizabeth Woollett.

Advertisement

As much as women’s bodies and their processes have been medicalised and pathologised, so too have female hormonal states tied to menstruation including perimenopause, menopause, premenstrual tension (PMT) and, more recently, the hormonal mental disorder known as premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). Photo: In her first work of non-fiction, Hell Days, Australian novelist Laura Elizabeth Woollett interrogates PMDD, or what she describes as “the inferno of hormonal mood disorder.” Interweaving memoir with investigative journalism and medical research, she explores the condition in several ways: the articulation of her own experience, research into the correlation between the menstrual cycle and mood disturbances, and interviews with fellow sufferers, as well as doctors and research scientists. With the benefit of diagnosis, treatment and hindsight, Woollett writes with clear-eyed honesty about her own jarring, cyclical experiences with PMDD. She remembers, for example, sitting under the harsh fluorescent lighting of the call centre where she worked, actively deciding to avoid taking the train to and from her job because of the depression and suicidal ideation with which she was struggling. She did not, she reveals, trust herself not to jump in front of a train. Likewise, she chronicles many years of emotional (and likely also hormonal) destabilisation, including struggles with mood fluctuations, body image and eating disordered behaviours, that she only correlated with her menstrual cycle while on holiday with her husband in Thailand in 2018. Feelings of heavy depression and vivid death fantasies plagued her until her period came and suddenly, she writes, “I felt fine again.”

Advertisement

She googled “PMS rage depression” and found information about PMDD. It was only then that she became aware of the condition which can cause severe emotional and physical changes before a woman’s period. Symptoms of the disorder can include, but are not limited to, depression, anger, irritability, difficulty concentrating, insomnia, lethargy, feelings of being out of control and suicidality. Most disturbingly, the illness is estimated to affect as many as one in 20 women, one in three of whom will attempt suicide. Related Article Literature Barbara Kingsolver’s hymn to Appalachia and the healing power of art As Woollett’s extensive research and interdisciplinary approach to her topic makes clear, relatively little that is concrete or scientifically verified is known about PMDD. Indeed, it was only in 2013 that the condition was formally moved out of the appendix of the psychiatric bible, the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM), and recognised as a stand-alone depressive diagnostic category. Treatment for the illness remains frustratingly experimental with doctors recommending sufferers take some form of oral contraception, antidepressant medication, hormone replacement therapy or even consider a hysterectomy, and research is predictably underfunded. More needs to be done, clearly, and that urgency underlies the wide-ranging discussions Woollett has with general practitioners, obstetricians and gynaecologists, psychologists and psychiatrists, scientists and researchers, as well as fellow sufferers.

Advertisement

Woollett’s accomplished and deeply impressive book is the second to be published in Australia this year on PMDD and sits comfortably alongside Emma Hardy’s insightful and personal Periodic Bitch as an important exploration of a medical condition that is both affecting vast numbers of women and radically diminishing the quality of their physical and mental health. Ultimately, what both volumes demonstrate is not only the depth and breadth of women and their suffering but that, at the intersection of menstrual and mental health, healthcare providers and broader healthcare systems worldwide are continuing to fail women in their responses to and treatment of their pain. title: The former Irish jumps jockey taking on Australia’s biggest stables in the Derby
text:

SportRacingSpring racing carnival The former Irish jumps jockey taking on Australia’s biggest stables in the Derby Andrew Wu October 30, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. When former jumps jockey Shane Jackson stepped out on his own as a trainer two years ago, he had just four horses in his stable, and 40 boxes to fill. “We had a big empty barn,” Jackson recalled this week. “It was a bit daunting early days.” Trainer Shane Jackson works Victoria Derby hopeful King Snitz in Warrnambool’s Lady Bay. Nicole Cleary Passionate racing identity Tony Ottobre was one of the many owners the Irishman messaged to ask for a horse. Years ago, he had ridden a jumps winner for Ottobre – whose mare Pride Of Jenni is one of Australia’s most popular racehorses – and he was using that as an in. It worked – sort of. Ottobre preferred to send his horses to trainers closer to his home on the peninsula, Jackson was told, and Warrnambool was too far away. Anyhow, he did not have a horse.

Advertisement

Out of the blue about a month later, Jackson said, he received another text from Ottobre, telling the fledgling trainer he had a young colt that was too small to take to the sales. “He had mostly fillies and mares at home and didn’t have the room for him so he said, ‘would you take him and break him in, do what you need to do’,” Jackson said. King Snitz will be trainer Shane Jackson’s first runner in a group 1 race. Nicole Cleary That colt was King Snitz, who on Saturday will be Jackson’s first runner in a group 1 race – in the $3 million Victoria Derby, no less, against the behemoth stables of Ciaron Maher, Chris Waller and Gai Waterhouse. Jackson’s road to the top started in Baltinglass, an Irish town about 60 kilometres south-west of Dublin. A champion claiming jumps jockey in Ireland, their version of an apprentice, Jackson rode in the major festivals at Cheltenham and Aintree.

Advertisement

But the rides dried up during Europe’s economic crisis in the early 2010s, forcing him, his wife Lauren and their young son Joseph to move to Australia in 2012. “The mortgage was getting higher to pay,” Jackson said. “It was either going off to find a different career path or go on an adventure.” They chose the latter. Their initial plan was to stay for three or four years, then make a call. Two more kids later, with another on the way, Jackson and his wife are still here, and dreaming big. Shane Jackson’s King Snitz is one of the leading chances in the Victoria Derby. Nicole Cleary Jackson was among the top hoops in his adopted home. His best seasons came in 2018-19 and 2019-20 when he won back-to-back Tommy Corrigan Medals for the state’s leading jumps jockey. He retired in 2021, aged just 34 and at the top of his game.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

Melbourne Cup Joy for Jamie Melham after late Melbourne Cup scratching: Who’s in the field and who can win His decision was met with surprise, but Jackson wanted to bow out on a high, and free of any life-changing injuries. He was also eager to start the next stage of his racing career. “A lot of sportspeople probably go on for too long, I went out with people wondering why I was giving it away, but I was thinking about training,” Jackson said. Jackson is among the growing number of jumps jockeys aiming to make it as trainers. He’s following in the footsteps of champion trainer Ciaron Maher and rising star Gavin Bedggood, who won this year’s Caulfield Cup with Kingswood. Maher, who started in Warrnambool and for whom he rode a winner, is an inspiration.

Advertisement

“There’s one place these guys want to get and that’s the top,” Jackson said. “If you don’t want to strive to be like that, and you’re happy to rest on your laurels and just be a mediocre trainer – that’s not my goal. “I’d love to on some day be a Ciaron Maher or Chris Waller. We just want to get bigger and get better quality horses and more winners.” Loading The life of a jumps jockey lends itself to becoming a trainer. Often, they do not make enough in prizemoney so need to subsidise their income by working in a stable, giving them a broader understanding of what it takes behind the scenes to get a horse on the track. “It’s not like being a flat jockey, that’s why they reckon jumps jockeys make good trainers in Australia,” Jackson said.

Advertisement

Jackson spent about five years with the former Warrnambool father-son training partnership of Bill and Symon Wilde, “breaking horses on the side” while riding full-time. He has also worked briefly for Darren Weir before his disqualification and in Lindsey Smith’s stables. Though he has held a trainer’s licence since 2022, it was not until 2024 that Jackson went out on his own. Though the challenging early days when he had more empty boxes than horses are gone, his is by no means a major stable. He has about 50 horses on the books, primarily based in Warrnambool with some at Flemington. His staff list has grown to 20. His wife, who works for Bendigo Bank by day, takes care of billing and accounts by night. “We’ve built pretty quick, which is great,” Jackson said. “Just work hard, keep the winners coming so we can keep expanding.” View post on X

Advertisement

King Snitz is the stable star, and Jackson’s first winner at group level after victory in the Norman Robinson Stakes (2000m), a traditional Derby lead-up race. Related Article Updated

Melbourne Cup Leading Melbourne Cup chance ruled out, four runners face a nervous wait Jackson loved the colt from the start. Even from the breaking in process, Jackson could tell King Snitz had a big tank. “[He’s] not the simplest horse to deal with, but you’d never get to the bottom of him when he was at the breaker,” Jackson said. “He was light-framed, small, carrying me around at 70 kg, and you still wouldn’t get him tired. “From day one we liked him. It was a waiting game then to get him to grow and develop and get him to the races.”

Advertisement

The plan this spring was to run King Snitz “two or three” times before tipping him out to the paddock but as his form lifted with the rise in distance, the goals became loftier. “It’s everyone’s dream to win a group 1, no doubt we’ll get there,” Jackson said. “If we could do that in the Derby this Saturday, it’d be amazing. It’d be a wee bit surreal, I suppose, but I think we do have a great chance. “If we can get a group 1 winner knocked off it will definitely help the business and attract better quality horses, and we can feature in these sort of races a bit more often.” Follow our Derby Day live blog from 11am Saturday and stick around for the Melbourne Cup barrier draw on Saturday evening. title: ‘It’s just a computer, right?’ How AI is tearing Gen Z in two
text:
Advertisement

LifestyleHealth & wellnessMental health ‘It’s just a computer, right?’ How AI is tearing Gen Z in two Tori Malek October 30, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. More than two-thirds of young people are struggling to unwind and feel an increasing sense of uncertainty around the future of artificial intelligence, while cost of living remains the number one concern for Australians aged 18 to 24, according to a new national survey. The annual Gen Z Wellbeing Index, released this week, found that 69 per cent of young Australians feel guilty for relaxing, citing worries around wasting time or feeling that they should be doing something deemed to be productive instead. Two-thirds of Australian Gen Zers said they feel guilty about resting. iStock University student Alyssa Mortimore, 19, said that despite knowing the importance of unwinding, she often felt stressed from doing too much and struggled to take a break. “You’re seeing so many people at times who are overworking themselves to the point where they’re not able to do anything,” she said. “I find I’m still guilty of doing that sometimes as well.”

Advertisement

Despite her peers’ attitudes, Mortimore said taking rest seriously had become something that most helped her adjust to life in Melbourne after moving from the small Tasmanian town of Huonville two years ago. Related Article Opinion

Dating My generation has lost the ability to date in real life. Dating apps aren’t helping Saria Ratnam Student “To go into a big city where your face can practically disappear was very, very jarring,” she said. “It was quite stressful, and I truthfully had a lot of anxiety attacks, which was not enjoyable.” Since then, Mortimore has made hobbies and relaxation – without the expectation of it being productive – a non-negotiable in her schedule. “I really love doing art, especially when I’m not going through the best time mentally,” said Mortimore. “Or if I can’t make art because I’m feeling burnt out, I will just listen to new music.”

Advertisement

Professor of wellbeing science at the University of Melbourne Nikki Rickard said that while experiencing periods of boredom and mental quietness might feel foreign, it is essential for young people’s development and wellbeing. “Mentally, emotionally, even socially – to be able to have time on your own and not depend always on back and forth between other people is a critical part of our natural development,” she said. Dhananjay Nagpal said he uses AI to reassure himself. Jason South Research from the University of Sydney earlier this year found the number of mental disorders in those aged 16 to 24 has surged from 23.4 per cent in 2007 to 36.2 per cent in 2022 – a relative increase of about 54 per cent. Of the survey respondents, one in four (26 per cent) reported they could not manage more than three hours without their phone.

Advertisement

Concerns about the cost of living was ranked as the number one issue for the third year in a row, followed by housing and rental affordability, and mental health. Related Article Opinion

Superannuation House poor, super rich: The one area young Australians are winning Victoria Devine Money columnist The prevalence of AI and concerns about its societal impact was listed as the fourth-most significant concern this year – up from 10th place in 2025. While 34 per cent of participants worried about how AI would impact the future jobs market, one in four Gen Zers turned to AI when in need of life advice. Traditionally, Rickard said, “young people are pretty bad at seeking help for their mental health”, noting that AI technology has helped fill the gaps where stigma or accessibility to services act as a barrier for seeking professional support.

Advertisement

“That’s where AI tools and digital tools offer a level of personalisation that can be really helpful, particularly for marginalised groups,” she said. However, Rickard stressed the importance of using specialised AI tools that have been rigorously trained as professionals are. Dhananjay Nagpal, 20, is studying computer science at the University of Melbourne and said he mostly uses AI for academic purposes, but sometimes to reflect on his own thoughts. “Not asking for advice, but maybe just reassuring myself,” he said. “But again, it’s just a computer, right? So you can’t really trust it.”

Advertisement

University of Melbourne critical thinking researcher Dr Samantha-Kaye Johnston said personalised general-purpose AI systems appeal to young people “because they’re quite convincing in terms of how they anticipate their needs, and they’re available 24/7”. But she warned that in order to be genuinely beneficial to a person’s development, AI chatbots and coaches need to be designed to provide cognitive friction, “which is the intellectual effort that’s involved in questioning information and being comfortable in encountering competing perspectives instead of just immediately receiving an answer”. Johnston said it comes down to encouraging young people to reach a level of autonomy to know when to turn away from chatbots for guidance, and providing them with the skills and tools to know how to turn towards the humans in their lives. "These actions have left David and One Nation deeply concerned that the government is seeking to use taxpayer funds to exert undue political influence over politicians," Hanson said in a statement on Thursday.

The offer comes as the Labor government seeks to fight off a surge in the polls by the populist One Nation, which has also eaten into the voting base of the right-leaning Coalition.

Farley has never publicly ruled out moving to Labor and once even tried to stand as a candidate for the party in 2021, having once also been a member of the Nationals.

"If she's already having trouble keeping her party together, that says something about her."

The One Nation leader has repeatedly issued the prime minister pleas for more staff, even teaming up with fierce political rival Fatima Payman in September to call for an overhaul of how personnel are divvied up among parliamentarians.

"This is One Nation yet again just trying to politicise an issue that shouldn't be about politics ... this is a storm in the teacup, and One Nation is just desperate to distract."

Farley's electorate of Farrer in southern NSW, which he won from the Liberals in a May by-election, is the second largest in the state, just slightly smaller than Greece.

title: Star Trek and X-Men star Patrick Stewart dies aged 86
text:
In brief Patrick Stewart was an accomplished Shakespearean stage actor before taking the sci-fi roles that made him a household name.

The actor was knighted in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Patrick Stewart, who rose from poverty in England to become an accomplished Shakespearean stage actor and then achieved global stardom as the erudite captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and the telepathic professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men movies, has died at the age of 86.

Stewart, knighted in 2010 by Queen Elizabeth for his contributions to drama, died at his home in Los Angeles, according to a statement on his X account.

"We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia," it said.

Stewart became an actor at age 18 and gained acclaim on the stage as a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company from the 1960s.

But it was not until after he was hired at age 47 for Star Trek: The Next Generation — a TV series that ran from 1987 to 1994 as a sequel to the original 1960s Star Trek — that he gained mainstream fame, acting into his 80s.

"Make it so," his character Picard often said, instructing a subordinate to carry out a command, or sometimes deploying the similar catch phrase, "engage".

It was a role he had debated taking after his longtime friend and fellow Shakespearean, Ian McKellen, advised him to spurn Star Trek and remain in theatre.

Stewart did take the role and became both a fan favourite and an indispensable part of a lucrative sci-fi franchise, playing Picard not only in 176 episodes over seven seasons of that series but also in several Star Trek films and in the later streaming series Star Trek: Picard that began airing in 2020 when he was 79.

"As the seven seasons of TNG went by, the distinction between Jean-Luc Picard and Patrick Stewart became thinner and thinner, until it was impossible for me to know where he left off and I began. So much of what I believed and felt went into that show," Stewart told the Guardian in 2022.

Stewart also initially baulked at being cast as the wheelchair-using mutant Professor X in the X-Men movies, based on the popular Marvel comic book character.

"I said, 'Look, I know this isn't science fiction, but it's fantasy, and I've done that.' But they persuaded me that it wouldn't be like Star Trek, so I did it. And yet again I was proved wrong," Stewart told the Guardian.

He became a critical part of another big-money franchise, starting with the first entry, X-Men, in 2000, followed by several more.

Stewart was born on 13 July, 1940, in the English town of Mirfield in Yorkshire.

He was raised in poverty, with a father who he said returned from World War Two an alcoholic who suffered from post-traumatic stress syndrome and physically abused Stewart's mother. Stewart recalled putting his body between his father and mother to try to protect her.

As a child, Stewart said, acting became a "safe space" after a schoolteacher introduced him to Shakespeare —specifically The Merchant of Venice — during a class when he was 12.

He started losing his hair at age 17 and was bald by 19. He was embarrassed at the time, but eventually embraced it.

title: What's really behind the numbers? The COVID legacy that's raising new questions
text:
in brief Without a reliable test, some Long COVID cases could be underreported, leading to knock-on effects.

Australia has a handful of Long COVID clinics run by hospitals or GPs in NSW, Victoria, SA and the ACT.

Long COVID may have affected fewer people for less time than previously thought new research suggests.

Using refined data collection methods, a team from Stanford University in the United States has found that people suffering from chronic COVID-like symptoms may have been misdiagnosed or the illness overreported.

According to the Australian government, Long COVID is defined as contracting COVID-19 and experiencing symptoms for a period of at least 12 weeks afterwards.

But researchers said no clinical test exists for Long COVID, making it difficult to track its prevalence accurately.

They stress that people who were wrongly assumed to have Long COVID may still have experienced debilitating symptoms that could have been caused by other illnesses.

"These findings indicate that Long COVID may be more similar to other extended post-viral syndromes than many have thought," said co-author Steven Goodman, professor of epidemiology and population health in the Stanford School of Medicine.

The Australian government predicted there would be more than 1.3 million cumulative historical Long COVID cases nationwide by the end of 2023 and suggested between 5-10 per cent of people who contract COVID-19 still have symptoms after three months.

How was the research done?

The Stanford researchers reviewed 4.4 billion health insurance records from more than 244 million Americans and say they found a flaw in previous studies.

Older research compared people who tested positive for COVID-19 with people who were never diagnosed or tested.

The issue is that people who are more likely to test also have more records of various health issues, which can create a biased association between those health issues and COVID-19.

Professor Jure Leskovec, another author of the study, explained these discrepancies may substantially overestimate the range and duration of health effects attributable to COVID-19.

"Our new study design found 98 per cent fewer Long COVID-attributable outcomes between four to 12 months after infection compared with conventional approaches applied in the same dataset," he said.

"This doesn’t mean Long COVID is 98 per cent less common. It means that how we design these studies fundamentally changes which health effects we can reliably attribute to COVID."

READ MORE Researchers discover new clue that helps explain severe COVID-19

By focusing only on patients who tested positive or negative, the researchers believe they have produced a more accurate picture of COVID-19's long-term health effects.

Professor Paul Griffin from the University of Queensland School of Medicine told SBS News refining our understanding of Long COVID is vital for supporting people with the illness.

"We need to make sure that we continue to look into Long COVID, manage those people, try and find tests and obviously also therapies to try and improve their situation," he said.

Difficulties with diagnoses

No diagnostic test exists for Long COVID, and Griffin explained that the criteria some experts use have shifted over time.

It's suspected there could even be different forms of Long COVID, further complicating both diagnosis and treatment.

"It's a complex constellation of symptoms that can involve pretty much every organ system in the body," Griffin said.

The disease can also manifest differently in people or be confused with other illnesses with similar symptoms.

In the worst case, some patients may have their symptoms dismissed or discounted because there is no reliable test.

"They may see some clinicians who say that they don't have anything wrong with them or that it might be due to something else or perhaps it's psychological and not an actual condition relating to their COVID infection."

Experts warn against losing sight of long COVID

Without a reliable test, some Long COVID cases could be underreported, which could mean inadequate resources are directed toward the condition.

"For a short period of time there were some resources deployed to help address that. But then I think in more recent times, a lot of those have been wound up," Griffin said.

Australia has only a handful of Long COVID clinics run by hospitals or GPs.

Dozens more of these clinics and targeted support programs have been discontinued since the height of the pandemic.

Experts said scientists worldwide will keep improving their understanding of the COVID-19 pandemic, both to better understand its impact and to prepare for future public health emergencies.

"COVID-19 had been one of the worst pandemics we face, but it certainly won't be the last. We can take the opportunity to reflect, see how we can be better prepared, and I guess also continue to manage COVID well," Griffin said.

Scrutinising and refining statistics is therefore part of building population wellbeing and resilience.

Leskovec said: "These results should complement physicians’ clinical assessments, not replace them."

"On the other hand, for data scientists, earlier Long COVID studies might need to be revisited with better controls. Our approach could improve those and future population-health studies."

title: Flattened by trains, targeted by vigilantes. Now, delivery robots face Australia
text:
In brief US firm Serve Robotics has launched self-driving robotic food delivery vehicles in Queensland.

Experts say the coming wave of automation will bring both disruption and benefit.

Australia's first delivery robots have begun their autonomous conquest of the Gold Coast's pavements, with experts saying that they could herald a new era in human-robot relations.

United States-based firm Serve Robotics has partnered with DoorDash to deliver meals on robotic wheels to local residents in Queensland, but the technology still has a long way to go before it becomes commonplace elsewhere in the country.

The robots, which carry takeaway orders on pavements at walking pace, are the same as those used by the company and its competitors in the US. They can access an operations depot at Griffith University.

Japan, Colombia, Germany, and others are also in various stages of rolling out autonomous delivery with other companies; however, the droids have not always been warmly received by residents.

In the US, where resentment towards the construction of data centres and the increasing ubiquity of artificial intelligence is growing, residents in places like Chicago, Los Angeles, and Philadelphia have filmed themselves attacking the robots.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Retired professor Carolyn Marvin was arrested earlier this month after a campaign of protest in which she deliberately stood in front of the machines to stop them doing their jobs. She said she was concerned that robots could soon replace human workers.

Elsewhere, delivery robots have been seen causing damage and chaos when their programming fails to match up with the environment around them.

There have been reports of broken-down robots blocking pavements, stopping at pedestrian crossings as emergency vehicles try to pass, and even running through glass bus stops.

In one viral incident, a robot was filmed straying onto railway lines before being flattened by an oncoming train.

Australians may hold similarly hostile views about the rise of the machines, given backlash against AI and concerns about data centres.

However, Australia Post's experiments with similar autonomous vehicles in 2017 did not spark major pushback.

Robots must overcome barriers

Professor Michael Milford, director of the QUT Centre for Robotics, told SBS News that an autonomous robotic future is by no means guaranteed.

"There's a number of challenges," Milford said. "There's societal acceptance. There's the perception of hogging precious space on the footpath, getting in people's ways occasionally, occasionally driving into bus shelter windows and all that sort of stuff.

"But ultimately, it's a commercial play by these companies, and there is, as far as I can tell, a very challenging path to being sufficiently profitable."

At present, the use of delivery robots is limited. However, analysts expect to see a spike in their adoption over the coming decade. Research firm Transforma Insight reported last year that 2.1 million could be operating worldwide by 2034.

Customers will be able to opt in or out of the robot delivery program starting on Thursday. Credit: Supplied

Although fears about job replacement by technology are widespread, Milford notes that the current food delivery system has its own issues — and is quite efficient.

Without being able to offer some advantage to hand-delivered takeout through price, speed, or otherwise, Milford said the robots face an uphill battle.

Yet, while challenges remain, there are also benefits, such as the removal of cars from the road.

"A lot of [these issues] come down to not the specific technology but to underlying societal things around capitalism and what people will accept," he said.

"This is sort of the pointy end of it, but a lot of this is true of any new technological development."

Productivity gains give robots advantage

While Serve Robotics' vehicles are currently delivering meals from just a single restaurant — Gnocchi Gnocchi, Southport — more are set to join soon.

DoorDash has said the robots are expected to complement its existing delivery drivers by completing short trips in dense urban environments, while humans continue to do longer, cross-city trips.

Professor Hai Vu, head of the Monash Connected Autonomous Vehicle program, told SBS News that automating aspects of the economy is largely inevitable given the productivity benefits on offer.

His team built Australia's first domestically designed and autonomous food-delivery robot in 2025, which they named ARI. Vu said their approach could solve some of the economic issues facing similar machines at present.

"Our approach is actually quite very different," Vu said, explaining that his machines do all of their computing remotely, rather than inside the vehicle as most others do.

"That enables us to have a very simple and low-cost robot," he said. "You could actually scale up thousands of these robots at a fraction of the cost."

Coming to a town near you?

Delivery robots are not automatically legal to operate in Australia and face a raft of regulatory roadblocks, with local councils at the forefront of how they might be regulated.

Gold Coast City Council has been working actively with technology companies and Griffith University to establish how autonomous robots might work on its streets.

Experts at Swinburne University and Monash are also mapping low-speed urban zones where delivery robots and humans might co-exist peacefully.

Milford said that the issues need to be thought through carefully, but that there is little reason Australia couldn't see more robots on its streets soon.

"If you can walk around [a robot], that's fine. But if you're in a wheelchair, for example, that could be catastrophically bad," he said.

"Technically and economically, there is no reason why you couldn't roll out a Waymo service in Sydney tomorrow," he said, referring to the driverless cars operating in the US.

Legally, NSW prohibits the use of fully autonomous vehicles, but Premier Chris Minns has publicly supported the idea, and Waymo — owned by Alphabet, Google's parent company — appears to be preparing to establish a presence in Australia.

"I would not be surprised at all if there was an announcement from Waymo or one of the other organisations that they're going to roll out trials in Sydney in 2027 or 2028," Milford said.

"Elsewhere, I expect to see gradual, steady expansion of these robo-taxis in a lot of places."

While the rollout may be slow, experts say it is coming. Hai cautioned policymakers that they need to play a more active role in addressing how the nation deals with the autonomous future rushing toward it, in order to both mitigate the impacts and reap the benefits.

"If you want to develop the economy," Hai said, "then you need to have the right incentives and provide the right opportunities for people to capitalise on those incentives."

title: A familiar political crisis could be looming as Israel counts its votes
text:
In brief Israel voted five times in less than four years between 2019 and 2022, as alliances repeatedly fell apart.

Neither side currently has a clear path to a majority - uncomfortable deals and potential deadlock could follow.

Israel has just voted, but the country could face another election within months if its deeply divided political parties fail to negotiate alliances to form a new government.

Israelis know this scenario all too well. Between 2019 and 2022, the country held five elections in less than four years, as coalitions repeatedly struggled to assemble majorities or fell apart once they did.

With around 90 per cent of votes from Wednesday's election counted, neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, have enough seats in their coalitions to assemble a majority.

Netanyahu's bloc is projected to win 53 seats, while Eisenkot's opposition is set for 48, though these figures may still change. The threshold for a majority is 61.

Meanwhile, two Arab parties — the Joint List and Ra'am — are on course for a historic combined 19 seats, potentially handing them significant influence over who forms the next government. But neither side has expressed willingness to work with them, limiting the Jewish blocs' paths to a majority.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Maybe everybody lost in these elections but the Arab parties. And for the Arab parties, it's unclear that they can make use of their huge success," Hebrew University of Jerusalem political scientist Gideon Rahat said.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog is now tasked with choosing a leader with the best chance of forming a government, with input from each party.

"We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections," he said after early results arrived, urging parties to keep "an open mind".

Israeli politics is known for its twists, turns and unlikely alliances, and many different scenarios could play out in the weeks to come — including a very real possibility of a stalemate that could take months to resolve.

So what happens if neither side can form a government?

The struggle to govern Israel

No party has ever won enough seats to govern Israel alone, forcing leaders to negotiate alliances with other parties.

Eisenkot faces particularly difficult choices, including the prospect of working with Netanyahu in a unity government, or with Arab parties, both of which he said he would not do.

His bloc includes both right-wing parties and the left-wing Democrats, the only Jewish party open to partnering with Arab-led parties.

Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen has indicated he would support an opposition government to oust Netanyahu without formally joining it, potentially opening the door to a fragile minority government.

But working with Arab parties could cost Eisenkot the support of right-wing allies, leaving him with few straightforward paths to power.

Netanyahu's options for partnerships appear more limited. Neither the Arab parties nor any of those in the opposition bloc have expressed willingness to work with him, though in Israeli politics, it's never wise to say never.

"As they say, politics is the art of the possible. In Israeli politics, it's the art of the unimaginable," Ran Porat, an Israel and Middle East lecturer and analyst at Monash University, told SBS News.

A stalemate could benefit Netanyahu

A prolonged political deadlock could work in Netanyahu's favour, allowing him to remain caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed.

That prospect has raised questions about how he might use his powers in the interim, particularly amid speculation over a renewed Israeli attack on Iran.

In the days leading up to the election, Netanyahu called for the overthrow of Iran's government. Media reports, which he denied, suggested senior military officials had pushed back against his plans to strike Iran ahead of the vote.

Following the election, Eisenkot warned Israel's security chiefs against allowing Netanyahu to put his political survival ahead of the national interest.

Porat says another deadlock could also result in lower turnout in a future election, disillusioning voters who turned out in force for this vote.

"The side that is anti-Netanyahu, the Arab sector, and the liberals, will be much less motivated to go and vote after they made this enormous effort this time around and did not reach a victory," he said.

Israel has been here before

In the April 2019 election, Netanyahu's party tied with the Blue and White alliance led by Benny Gantz, both securing 35 seats.

But efforts to form a government failed amid disagreements over military conscription exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jews, triggering another election in September.

That vote also failed to produce a government.

A third election in March 2020 eventually resulted in a unity government between Gantz and Netanyahu who agreed to share the prime ministership on a rotating basis.

That government collapsed after less than a year over a budget dispute, before Gantz could take his turn as leader, prompting a fourth election in March 2021.

That vote produced an unlikely eight-party coalition spanning the political spectrum — including an Arab Islamist party for the first time — bring Netanyahu's premiership to an end.

The government was led initially by the right-wing Naftali Bennett and later the centrist Yair Lapid under a power-sharing agreement. But the coalition struggled to reconcile its ideological differences and lost its majority.

Its collapse saw Lapid take over as caretaker prime minister ahead of a fifth election in November 2022, which returned Netanyahu to power.

Lessons for Eisenkot

Porat says the lessons from the last political crisis "have been internalised [by Eisenkot] quite significantly".

He said the collapse of the previous anti-Netanyahu coalition highlighted the importance of party loyalty over ideology, after several right-wing politicians broke ranks, leading to the breakdown of the government.

"So the first lesson is to get people who are loyal to you, which they did, on Eisenkot's side," he said.

The second lesson, he added, is to avoid addressing how to resolve issues with Palestinians, particularly in the West Bank.

"Because if there's something that all parties disagree about ... is what should be done with the settlements and possibly future annexation or compromise."

That issue is "toxic" for the anti-Netanyahu bloc, he explained, particularly if it ultimately ends up including an Arab party.

Views across such a coalition could range anywhere from calling for an immediate two-state solution to annexing the West Bank.

Eisenkot has been cautious about articulating a long-term vision for Palestinians during his campaign, though he has rejected the prospect of a two-state solution under current conditions while opposing Israeli annexation of the occupied West Bank.

Many analysts say it's unlikely, even under a new government, that there will be any significant progress towards territorial compromises with Palestinians in the immediate future.

"Avoid that [issue] at all costs, because that will break down the government," Porat said.

title: How a Kylian Mbappé 'dictator' meme prompted a Real Madrid apology to China
text:
In brief French footballer Kylian Mbappé and Real Madrid apologised after comments about Mao Zedong sparked backlash in China.

Chinese broadcasters and sponsors cut ties as outrage over the remarks spread online.

Real Madrid has apologised to China after star striker Kylian Mbappé apparently joked about Mao Zedong in comments that sparked a social media storm and saw Spanish football yanked off state TV.

Mocking former leader Mao is taboo in China, and Mbappé's remarks saw him become the latest foreign sports figure to anger the country.

In a clip of a video interview with French show The Bridge — since taken down — Mbappé talked about being amused by an internet meme of his face photo-shopped onto "some guy, think he's a Chinese dictator", an apparent reference to Mao.

The fallout was immediate. Chinese beverage giant Dongpeng, which during this year's World Cup ran adverts with AI-generated images of Mbappé, said on Tuesday it had scrapped its partnership with the player, as did dairy firms Mengniu and Milkground.

CMG, which oversees public broadcaster CCTV, said it had suspended broadcasts of La Liga, the world's second-richest football league after England's Premier League.

On Wednesday, Real Madrid issued a statement saying it "wishes to express its apologies to the Chinese people for any offence caused by the recent remarks of our player Kylian Mbappé".

"The club joins in the public apology issued by Kylian Mbappé, in which the player himself expressed his regret for his words and reiterated his respect for the Chinese people," the 15-time European champions said.

The statement came a day after Mbappé — who was the top scorer in this year's World Cup with 10 goals — issued his own apology, saying: "My comment was ill-judged and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world."

Mbappé made the comments while speaking with French show The Bridge. Source: Supplied

Foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a regular briefing on Wednesday: "We take seriously the apology the individual concerned has made."

La Liga said on Tuesday it "deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé's recent comments have caused among Chinese fans".

Earlier, the Chinese state-run Global Times said in an editorial that it was "not difficult to see that the club's longstanding tolerance of such behaviour has contributed to Mbappé's latest offensive remarks".

Mbappé, 27, continued to face a torrent of criticism from Chinese web users on Wednesday, some of it racist.

"His remarks were hurtful toward China and the Chinese people, so they cannot be translated," wrote one user on social media platform Weibo.

Mbappé's original joke about Mao was not reposted — or had been scrubbed — from China's tightly controlled social media.

Drinks company Dongpeng was among the Chinese companies to cut ties with Kylian Mbappé. Source: Getty / Liu Junfeng

Chinese social media app Xiaohongshu had meanwhile frozen Mbappé's account, where he has over a million followers.

The same was done on the Weibo app, with a notice stating that "the user has been banned from following due to violating laws or the Weibo Community Convention".

Some Chinese media reports said global brands like Dior and Hublot had removed their Mbappé-related content on Weibo.

A search by the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency on Dior and Hublot's Weibo page with Mbappé's Chinese name produced no results.

'Respect history'

Offline too the Mbappé brand appeared to be under threat.

When AFP visited the Adidas flagship store in Beijing's Sanlitun shopping district, Real Madrid shirts were available for sale, but none bearing the striker's name.

Chinese state media have previously praised Mbappé as a "footballing sensation" and "talent".

His face is plastered on billboards, on soft drinks and across social media.

Kylian Mbappé had sponsorship deals with several Chinese companies that have scrapped the agreements following the controversy. Source: Getty / Future Publishing

Mbappé is sometimes affectionately referred to as "Guigui", meaning "turtle" in Chinese, for his resemblance to a character from the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles movie.

Other major overseas sports leagues have previously angered China.

China suspended sponsorship deals with the US National Basketball Association while the state broadcaster pulled NBA games off Chinese television for a year in October 2019.

This followed Houston Rockets executive Daryl Morey tweeting "Fight for freedom, stand with Hong Kong", referring to protests the Chinese government called separatist and seditious.

"Respecting the history, culture, social customs and national sentiments of others is a fundamental principle for cross-border interaction, a standard of conduct widely upheld by the international community," the official People's Daily newspaper said in an opinion piece.

title: Australia's $550 fuel hit is among world's highest
text:
In brief Australians have paid more than $500 extra for fuel amid the global fuel crisis.

Experts say that industry is driving Australia's reliance on diesel.

Surging fuel prices amid the war in the Middle East have cost Australians more than $500 per person on average, with the national impact of fuel price shocks exceeding $14 billion since March this year according to a report.

Australians have seen the third-highest fuel price increases compared to other countries, with individuals paying on average $546 more than usual, according to analysis from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).

The analysis, which compared average fuel prices in January to February, before the disruption of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, with prices during March to October, found that price shocks had cost 169 countries, including Australia, $665 billion.

The country paying the most amid global fuel shocks was the United States, with more than $226 billion in additional costs.

Americans paid an extra $666 per person, Canadians $597, and New Zealand's motorists followed close behind Australians at $484 per person.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Senior economist at the University of Sydney Luke Hartigan said Australia's position in the top four alongside Canada, the US and New Zealand made sense, considering Australia has the highest per capita diesel usage rates in the world, driven by high use in mining and farming.

"That's why similar patterns appear in the US, Canada and New Zealand, all of which have large agricultural sectors, and Canada also has a significant mining industry," Hartigan told SBS News.

Australia was among the top three countries for fuel expenditure per person, with the bulk of the cost coming from diesel. Source: SBS News / CREA

Geography was also an important factor, he said.

"Apart from New Zealand, these countries are vast, and distances between production centres and consumers are enormous."

"Moving fruit and vegetables from Queensland to Sydney, or freight from the Northern Territory to major cities, can involve distances comparable to crossing Europe."

Diesel costs blow out

Australia imports more than 90 per cent of its refined and crude oil, leaving it particularly vulnerable to fuel price shocks amid ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

But another issue contributing to Australia's vulnerability was its increasing use of diesel, which Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) CEO Amandine Denis-Ryan said was "really at odds" with the rest of the world.

"Between 2000 and recent years, Australia increased its diesel intensity by 33 per cent, while the world decreased it by 30 per cent, and countries like the US and Japan reduced it by 50 per cent," she told SBS News.

As the world's largest importer of diesel, Australia represents 10 per cent of the global seaborne diesel trade and is also the third-largest importer of petrol and jet fuel.

When compared with Australia's share of global GDP and population, Denis-Ryan said, "These numbers are enormous."

Australia paid almost $15 billion more for fuel from March to October. Source: SBS News / CREA

Diesel use has been trending upwards this century according to government figures, that show diesel comprises 44.1 per cent of transport energy use. It's the most used road and rail transport fuel and is a popular ship fuel.

"We've been shifting away from rail freight towards road freight, and we've also been shifting from underground coal mines, which mostly use electricity, to open-cut coal mines, which mostly use diesel," Denis-Ryan said.

And there are geological factors as well: "As we exhaust our best and most easily accessible mineral resources, we need more diesel for each tonne of coal produced and each tonne of ore produced," Denis-Ryan said, adding that Australia's vehicles were largely "really old and quite inefficient".

Australian households paying the price

Recent research from IEEFA assessed the link between inflation and oil shocks, and found that "in the last six inflation flare-ups in Australia since 2000, oil price shocks were a key contributor every time".

A reduction in the impact of oil price shocks on Australia's economy could provide broader economic benefits, Denis-Ryan said, noting that households would be less vulnerable to inflation if they switched to electric cars.

The CREA report found that while the US experienced enormous fuel costs, US electric vehicle (EV) drivers had seen just a $17 increase in charging costs since the start of March.

Hartigan said there has been an "enormous" uptake of EVs in Australia, starting at the height of the fuel crisis in March. Data from the National Australia Bank showed that EV loans doubled as Australians sought to dodge soaring petrol and diesel prices.

Senior economist at the left-wing thinktank the Australia Institute Matt Grudnoff said that governments could reduce or offset the upfront purchase cost of EVs.

But he said the bid to electrify Australia's roads should focus on industry.

"The public conversation tends to focus on household fuel costs because that's where people notice the impact most directly when they fill up their cars.

"But the data shows that a large share of the economic impact happens behind the scenes through freight and transport.

"Higher fuel prices increase the cost of moving goods around the country, which then contributes to inflation across the economy."

A move toward EVs

A recent report from the Climate Council found Australia paid more than twice as much as any other nation in additional diesel import costs during the global fuel crisis, putting the toll at $9 billion over six months.

Moves to renewable energy had saved Australians from some higher costs, the report found, with electric and hybrid cars cutting $1.7 billion in costs and saving the equivalent of 17.4 million litres of petrol and diesel per week.

Denis-Ryan said she hoped the fuel crisis would be a "wake-up call" for Australia, "particularly in terms of accelerating transport electrification, but also in looking at how we can slow the growth of oil use, and diesel use in particular, throughout Australia".

title: The $2.5 billion cancer bill Australia's sunscreen overhaul may not fix
text:
in brief The regulator is now developing reforms to strengthen sunscreen testing.

But experts say more reliable testing is only part of the solution.

Australia's sunscreen regulator is planning tougher rules after concerns some products failed to deliver the sun protection promised on their labels.

But experts say more reliable testing is only part of the solution, with boosting awareness on how Australians need to apply and reapply sunscreen also critical to preventing skin cancer.

In a report published last year, consumer group CHOICE tested 20 popular sunscreens and found that only four met their labelled sun protection factor (SPF), raising questions about the reliability of products Australians rely on to protect themselves from UV radiation.

The Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) later recalled several sunscreen products after identifying batches that didn't deliver their advertised SPF protection.

The regulator is now developing reforms to strengthen sunscreen testing, improve ingredient-quality requirements, and clarify the SPF claims cosmetic products can make.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

What are the proposed reforms?

The TGA is proposing several reforms to address sunscreen quality, with the goal of reducing instances of skin cancer.

Australia has the highest rate of melanoma incidence in the world, with an estimated 17,443 new cases diagnosed in 2025 according to Cancer Australia.

The reforms are:

Strengthen sunscreen testing requirements

Develop specific ingredient quality requirements

Provide a consistent limit for SPF rating that can be claimed for all secondary (cosmetic) sunscreens

Review sunscreen good manufacturing practice guidance

Consider labelling for SPF ratings

Professor Terry Slevin, CEO of the Public Health Association of Australia, told SBS News that treating skin cancers costs the country almost $2.5 billion each year.

"We need to invest more in preventing those cancers rather than having to treat them at the tail end," he said.

The TGA told SBS News: "The proposed reforms are intended to provide greater assurance through stronger testing requirements, increased oversight of testing laboratories, testing of finished products and periodic testing over a product’s lifecycle, and improved access by the TGA to SPF testing evidence."

Improving testing

Improving how sunscreen is tested is one way the TGA wants to improve quality and reliability of SPF claims.

Slevin explained that a small number of labs in Australia produce the nation's sunscreen, supplying multiple brands.

Sunscreens can then be tested on volunteers who use the formula and are then exposed to UV radiation; the rate at which skin reddens can then be used to determine the product's quality.

Experts say sunscreen safety is not just about the products, but also how we apply it. Source: AAP / Dan Himbrechts

While this method is common, it can also be imprecise.

"People have different skin types, and the amount of product being applied can vary a lot. So having consistent SPF levels relies on a lot of unpredictable variables," Slevin said.

These variations can lead to inconsistent product application and to sunscreens having marginally different SPF than advertised on their packaging.

Should you be worried about SPF levels?

The TGA reforms are looking to ensure that sunscreen manufacturers have clearer guidance and expectations, but SPF levels could still slightly vary from bottle to bottle according to Slevin.

However, variations would be minimal and would have little impact on the sunscreen's efficacy.

"The difference between SPF 50 and SPF 30 may sound significant, but the difference in the amount of UV that’s filtered out is only 3 per cent, a small change," he said.

"The vast majority of sunscreens serve a very useful and effective purpose; these reforms will only strengthen this."

But the main way to achieve the TGA's goal may not be reforming testing, but educating people on how to use sunscreen products best.

Dispelling confusion

Anna Wang, an associate professor in the School of Chemistry at UNSW Sydney, said that improving consumer understanding and behaviour is the best way to improve sun safety.

"What is going to make a bigger impact isn’t whether a sunscreen tests SPF45 using one method and SPF40 using another, but how often we reapply, and whether we put the recommended amount on," she told SBS News.

Experts recommended applying sunscreen generously to all exposed skin every two hours, seeking shade, and wearing a hat and sunglasses.

Towelling off after a swim, or wiping water or sweat off your body, can also remove some sunscreen.

Some cosmetic products, including foundations and moisturisers, also advertise SPF protection.

The TGA is considering a consistent limit on the SPF ratings these secondary sunscreens can claim, aiming to make it easier for consumers to distinguish products designed primarily for sun protection from those intended mainly for cosmetic use.

"In Australia, we have several hundred formulations to choose from so it can be confusing," Wang said.

She supported the TGA's reforms to clarify the distinction between primary and secondary sunscreens.

Investigation ongoing

In the meantime, the TGA confirmed to SBS News its investigation into sunscreens with disputed SPF results is ongoing.

"The TGA is considering the available evidence and providing sponsors with an opportunity to provide additional data or evidence before regulatory decisions are made," it told SBS News.

The regulator said it will issue product recalls or cancellations as needed while it develops the new reforms.

"The TGA intends to publish its findings and learnings and provide further guidance to sponsors and manufacturers to clarify expectations around SPF evidence and testing."

Clarification: This story has been revised to reflect the estimated $2.5 billion cost of skin cancer annually.

title: Inflation 'persisting longer' than desired, Treasurer says, after surprising spike
text:
In brief Core inflation rose faster than expected, adding to pressure on the Reserve Bank.

Fresh inflation data has fuelled expectations of another interest rate hike.

Core inflation climbed 1 per cent in Australia over the quarter, with the Reserve Bank governor warning underlying inflation is still too high.

The September quarter increase in the trimmed mean was in line with economists' expectations but exceeded the central bank's forecast of a 0.8 per cent increase.

On an annualised basis, the trimmed mean — a measure of underlying inflation that removes the biggest price swings — rose 3.6 per cent.

Headline inflation was hotter than expected by the market, at 1.3 per cent over the quarter.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers acknowledged inflation is persisting "longer than anyone would like" and citing the war in the Middle East as a major factor.

Markets had upped their bets for a November hike after comments in the past week by the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, and chief economist Sarah Hunter, indicating that inflation remained too high.

At the same time as the data was published by the Australian Bureau of Statistics, RBA governor Michele Bullock was appearing alongside Hauser, Hunter and other top officials at a Senate estimates hearing.

Elevated underlying inflationary pressures were a sign that the labour market was still tight, Bullock said.

"The Monetary Policy Board will meet next week," she said.

"We'll discuss our assessment of the flow of data and how the risks are unfolding. A key question is whether the tightening in monetary policy to date will be sufficient to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time."

Source: SBS News

Monthly headline inflation rose 4.3 per cent on an annual basis, up from 4 per cent in the 12 months to August.

"Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation in September, rising by 5.2 per cent," said Rachael McCririck, ABS head of price statistics.

Transport was the second largest contributor, rising by 8.7 per cent annually, due to higher fuel costs.

Fuel and the war in the Middle East

Speaking to press in Canberra, Treasurer Jim Chalmers issued a small mea culpa.

"We accept our part in the fight against inflation," Chalmers said.

"We take responsibility for government policy when it comes to the fiscal settings and when it comes to managing the budget in a responsible way in the face of this inflation challenge, which is persisting longer than anyone would like."

Chalmers again blamed rising inflation on higher fuel prices driven by the conflict in the Middle East.

"This war in the Middle East has been disastrous for Australians, for cost of living, and for inflation right around the world," he said.

"The point that [Treasury] secretary [Jenny] Wilkinson made today and the point that governor Bullock made today is that global energy prices are much higher than have been assumed. And we know what's driving that."

Speaking to reporters after Chalmers' conference, Opposition treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson said Australian families need the government to get inflation under control.

"There will be a lot of households, family, sitting around the kitchen tables of the nation figuring out — what is left to cut? Small business owners who will take this inflation data as a kick directly at their future opportunity and their hope."

title: 'The fire is out': Star casino's future in doubt after huge money laundering fine
text:
In brief Star Entertainment has been fined $260 million over historical money laundering failures.

The penalty leaves Australia's biggest listed casino operator facing an uncertain future.

Australia's biggest listed casino company is on the brink of administration after being fined $260 million for historical money-laundering violations.

The Star Entertainment Group was fined in the Federal Court on Wednesday, four years after financial intelligence agency AUSTRAC launched legal action against the company.

The agency previously argued a $400 million penalty was necessary to punish what it said were "manifest failures" at Star.

But the stockmarket-listed company, which has a market value of $763 million, argued any penalty over $100 million would send it into liquidation.

Justice Cameron Moore determined a $260 million penalty was appropriate for the significant harm Star's conduct has caused.

Star will have 19 months to pay the fine in four equal instalments.

Shares in the casino giant closed at 13 cents on Tuesday.

It is in a trading halt for up to two days to give management time to publicly address the fine's impact on the business.

Catholic parents in the Southern Highlands have been blindsided by a bishop’s decision to close their school in two years’ time. The move to shut down St Michael’s primary school in Mittagong, south of Sydney, comes against a backdrop of cost-cutting at Catholic schools across the state, but in this case, the local priest said the closure was due to declining enrolments with fewer families able to afford living in the area. St Michael’s at Mittagong will cease operations with students sent to another school in 2029. Google Earlier this year, more than a dozen northern beaches Catholic schools were told they would have to share a principal, while the Newcastle-Maitland diocese made over 50 school librarian jobs redundant. The sector’s overarching organisation, Catholic Schools NSW, has also been the subject of a corruption inquiry, which aired allegations that cash was used to branch stack right-wing Liberal Party factions.

Advertisement

Related Article Education Education boss to parents: Either share your principal, or pay $5000 extra a year On Thursday, families of the 180 students at St Michael’s Catholic Parish Primary School, Mittagong were told that in 2029 their school would be merged with St Thomas Aquinas Catholic Parish Primary School, Bowral, which is five kilometres away. Informing parents of the decision, the Bishop of Wollongong, Brian Mascord, branded the new arrangements “an amalgamation” of the two schools. The new school will be called Corpus Christi Catholic Parish Primary School and be located in the former St Thomas’ campus in Bowral. “I know this news may come as a shock and may bring uncertainty and concern for families,” he said in a letter on Thursday afternoon. “This is understandable and a testament to the great experience you and your family have had at St Michael’s or St Thomas Aquinas. At the same time, as Bishop, it is my responsibility to carefully consider and respond as best I can to the various needs of all people living in parishes within the diocese.”

Advertisement

He said the decision was made in response to a proposal from the Mittagong-Bowral parish, and factored in data, as well as consideration of the diverse needs of the people living in and around the parish. “At present, there are needs within the Mittagong-Bowral (and broader Southern Highlands) region that are going unmet,” he said. “While no decision has been made about how the site at Mittagong may be used from 2029, this change means the parish can explore options to meet broader community needs.” But that explanation made little sense to mother Jennifer Hogan, who chose St Michael’s for her children after moving to Mittagong from Sydney about a year ago.

Advertisement

One son is in kindergarten, and she previously had plans to enrol her two younger children at the school before the news. “The staff weren’t given any warning,” she said. “The whole thing feels gross: no consultation, no warning, and the information is convoluted.” “They’ve told us that a whole school is closing ... Is that because there is no other option? It doesn’t make sense – the Southern Highlands is booming. Why would you delete a whole school?” Corpus Christi Parish priest, Father Sean Cullen said on Friday the Bowral primary school had seen numbers decline steadily over a decade. Enrolment data shows they dropped from 380 a decade to 220 this year.

Advertisement

Related Article Education In selective schools, parental pressure is driving students to the psychologist’s office “And one of the reasons for that is [that] Bowral is an expensive place to live and people with young people can’t afford to live there,” he said. He said the decision would deliver “one vibrant school”. He said they considered moving the school to Mittagong but said the size of land of the Bowral primary school was bigger, but the deciding factor was the parish’s Bowral church was larger and could accommodate the entire school. So what is going to happen with the soon-to-be-empty school in Mittagong?

Advertisement

“We don’t know yet,” he said. “The Highlands has an older population, the demographics are quite elderly ... there could be a need for some care for the aged ... but we don’t know what’s happening with the site.” A Catholic Education Diocese of Wollongong spokesperson said neither the financial viability of either school, nor potential savings in education spending, played any role in the decision. “The amalgamation was not driven by cost reductions, but by a strategic response to a parish proposal following the 2021 merger of the Bowral and Mittagong parishes into Corpus Christi Catholic Parish. “The primary motivation is allowing the parish to address unmet pastoral and community needs in the Southern Highlands and maintain the ongoing viability of its ministries, while continuing to provide sustainable, high-quality Catholic education,” the spokesperson said.

Advertisement

The spokesperson said this week’s announcement marked the beginning of an in-depth consultation process where families, students, and staff would create the new school’s, identity, traditions, motto, and uniform. This week’s Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is…NGX Limited.. It was another week when Wall Street demonstrated its extraordinary ability to make mountains of money disappear, artificial intelligence continued its expensive march towards world domination and Australian mortgage holders wondered whether the Melbourne Cup might come with an unwelcome interest rate surprise. Google parent Alphabet supplied the week’s biggest disappearing act, shedding a mind-bending US$500 billion (A$694B) in market value as investors took fright at the astronomical cost of the artificial intelligence revolution. Half a trillion dollars up in smoke in a single session. That’s enough to buy a fair chunk of the ASX, with change left over for a five-hour lunch and a 1961 Château Latour. Apparently, even Google’s “super” intelligence didn’t see that one coming! The sell-off followed disappointing earnings and concerns about whether the enormous sums being poured into AI infrastructure will eventually produce profits large enough to justify the expenditure.

Advertisement

The technology might be getting smarter, but investors are increasingly interested in whether the people paying for it know their times tables. Not that the AI gravy train showed much inclination to slow down. Anthropic, the outfit behind the Claude chatbot, filed for a blockbuster initial public offering that could reportedly raise as much as US$100 billion (A$143B) and value the business at somewhere between US$1.5 trillion (A$2.13T) and US$2 trillion (A$2.84T). Its prospectus revealed US$16.3B (A$23.2B) in first-half 2026 revenue, alongside an eye-watering US$80.7B (A$114.7B) net loss, much of it reflecting changes in the “accounting value” of its convertible financing instruments. Apparently, the solution to spending mountains of money developing artificial intelligence is to ask punters for an even bigger mountain of cash.

Advertisement

The proposed float could challenge Elon Musk’s SpaceX for the title of history’s biggest IPO, although the final price tag remains anyone’s guess. And while investors were trying to work out what the AI revolution was actually worth, the Middle East supplied another reminder that markets have more than technology valuations to worry about. Israel’s parliamentary election failed to deliver a decisive majority, leaving Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to face difficult coalition negotiations in a region rarely renowned for political tranquillity. With neither major bloc securing the 61 seats needed to govern, another political stalemate now looms over a region where tensions involving Iran and neighbouring countries continue to cast a dark shadow over energy markets. And with inflation already proving stubborn, the world’s central bankers could probably do without another geopolitical food-fight.

Advertisement

Back home, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was discovering that political life can be a nasty bunker shot, whether navigating the hazards of climate diplomacy in Fiji or the fallout from a round of golf in his own backyard. Senate estimates revealed a staggering $34.6 million in contracted commitments for the Fiji Pre-COP climate summit, including a significant spend on accommodation and event management for the three-day event. Officials expect the “indefensible” bill to be lower, but taxpayers could be forgiven for wondering whether saving the planet comes with too much Kava and complimentary cocktails. And just as Albo might have hoped to escape the financial rough, the Marrickville Golf Club affair popped up. A $6.05 million federal grant to the club in his electorate, where he had held an undeclared honorary membership before hastily declining the honour once it became public, drew fresh scrutiny. The PM was then forced to walk back claims the money was intended to fix sewage – read: bulldust – problems after the NSW Government pointed out it was already footing the bill for those works. Instead, the federal largesse was earmarked for clubhouse renovations and other improvements, presumably to make the place a little more befitting of its prime ministerial patron.

Advertisement

Between the Pacific spending debate and the golf club controversy, Albo has certainly had a week of hitting political one-irons. Unfortunately for the Prime Minister, there are no “mulligans” in the house of Reps. And speaking of household budgets, mortgage holders had good reason to reach for the absinthe bottle ahead of Tuesday’s Melbourne Cup. Fresh inflation figures showed annual headline inflation reaching 4.3 per cent in September, with underlying inflation still above the Reserve Bank’s comfort zone. The latest numbers had economists contemplating another interest-rate increase, potentially lifting the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85 per cent on the very day the nation stops to watch the ponies thunder down the Flemington straight. While punters study the form guide for a winner, the Reserve Bank could be saddling up another rate hike. And just like backing a horse that falls at the 400, this one looks capable of leaving everyone a little lighter in the pocket.

Advertisement

With technology stocks wobbling, geopolitical tensions simmering and Australia’s interest-rate outlook highly uncomfortable, the speculative end of the ASX had plenty of excuses to pull up lame. But a few small-cap hopefuls clearly missed the memo. This week’s podium belonged to African gold explorer NGX Limited, Mozambique LNG contractor RBR Group and concrete technology developer Eden Innovations, with all three producing gains that would have shareholders reaching for the French rather than the Disprin. NGX Ltd’s team during a recent due diligence visit showing the optimum terrain for exploration activities at one of its freshly acquired gold prospects in Namibia’s Damara gold belt. NGX LIMITED (ASX: NGX)

Up 92.9% (7c – 13.5c) Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is African gold hopeful NGX Limited, which nearly doubled its share price after unveiling an ambitious move into Namibia’s highly prospective Damara Gold Belt. The explorer charged from seven cents to 13.5 cents after securing agreements to acquire majority interests in seven Namibian gold exploration licences covering more than 1300 square kilometres, giving it a substantial foothold in one of southern Africa’s established gold provinces. Its proposed portfolio includes the Erongo and Otjikoto South gold projects, with Erongo sitting near WIA Gold’s Kokoseb deposit, which reportedly hosts a whopping 3.78 million ounces of the yellow metal. The ground covers geological structures associated with gold mineralisation across the Damara Gold Belt, while Otjikoto South lies near B2Gold’s established 1.95-million-ounce Otjikoto gold mine.

Advertisement

NGX can initially earn 51 per cent interests in the relevant project companies, with staged agreements allowing ownership to increase to as much as 85 per cent on most licences. Acquisition terms include initial consideration of up to US$545,000 (A$774,000) and further staged payments of up to US$2.46M (A$3.5M) over seven years, alongside exploration funding commitments and licence tenure conditions. Not content with gold alone, the company also secured rights over the 194-square-kilometre Karas copper project, just 10 kilometres east of Koryx Copper’s Haib deposit, home to 5.3 billion pounds of contained copper. Karas hosts known copper occurrences, including the historically worked Sperlingputs prospect, giving NGX another exploration string to its African bow. To help finance its ambitions, the company completed a $3.6 million placement bookbuild at six cents per share, with directors or their nominees committing $540,000, subject to shareholder approval.

Advertisement

The proceeds are slated to support exploration across Namibia and Malawi, with initial work at Erongo expected to include soil and calcrete sampling, field-based gold analysis and geological target generation. Several licence transactions remain subject to approvals and tenure conditions, so there’s still a fair bit of dirt to turn before NGX can claim to have struck the mother lode. But with its shares almost doubling, the market clearly reckons the Namibian treasure hunt is worth buying a ticket for. RBR GROUP LIMITED (ASX: RBR) Up 53.3% (1.5c – 2.3c)

Snagging silver was Mozambique-focused RBR Group, which surged 53.3 per cent after landing its first contract at the country’s giant LNG developments since force majeure restrictions were lifted. The company’s Projectos Dinamicos subsidiary landed a US$2M (A$2.84M) subcontract to manufacture and deliver 32 accommodation modules and associated facilities for at least 100 workers at ExxonMobil’s Rovuma LNG project in northern Mozambique. The contract forms part of a broader US$7M (A$9.95M) accommodation package and represents the first stage of a development ultimately intended to house about 700 personnel. Manufacturing is scheduled to begin in early November, with delivery targeted for late January 2027. For RBR, which has spent years positioning itself to provide workforce services, training and infrastructure support to Mozambique’s gas industry, the deal represents a potentially important commercial breakthrough.

The country’s LNG developments have endured prolonged disruption from security concerns and project delays, leaving contractors waiting for major construction activity to resume. Now RBR has an actual contract to show for its persistence. And while A$2.84M might barely cover the morning coffee bill on a multibillion-dollar LNG development, it looks like a solid starting point for a small company establishing itself in the supply chain. RBR says Projectos Dinamicos and its Futuro Skills business are pursuing tender opportunities with a combined potential value of approximately US$100M (A$142M). Those opportunities are not yet secured revenue, but they offer a glimpse of the prize RBR hopes to chase as Mozambique’s gas sector gathers momentum.
