Successful delivery of the accommodation modules could strengthen the company’s credentials for future work, although additional contracts are far from guaranteed. After years of waiting for Mozambique’s LNG juggernaut to get moving, RBR has finally managed to get a foot in the door. text:

Australia’s staging of the Rugby League World Cup has been a raging success on the surface, drawing strong crowds and television ratings and already featuring an epic showdown between the Kangaroos and New Zealand. But behind the scenes, there is unrest about a landscape of haves and have-nots in the international game rearing its head. Loading Officials from some of the cash-strapped nations are disgruntled about having to fork out tens of thousands of dollars for corporate boxes at their own games to the Australian Rugby League Commission, the tournament organiser. ARL Commission executive chairman Peter V’landys has hosted guests in plush facilities at the Kangaroos’ two matches to date, against the Kiwis at Allianz Stadium and against Fiji at Brisbane’s Suncorp Stadium last Sunday.

Advertisement

But governing bodies from other nations have been forced to dig into limited funds to pay for corporate suites to entertain their VIPs and sponsors when their teams are playing, rather than having them provided by the World Cup hosts. On Friday, V’landys defended the planning for the tournament, pointing to the funds provided to competing nations. According to sources with knowledge of the issue, speaking on the condition of anonymity, Papua New Guinea officials even considered abandoning hosting games during the World Cup if boxes were not made available. Australia and New Zealand opened the tournament at Allianz Stadium before a crowd of 41,255. Getty Images There was heightened sensitivity over that situation given the Australian government is ploughing $600 million into the code to bankroll the incoming PNG Chiefs and the expansion of rugby league in the Pacific and ward off the influence of China in the region. In the end, the policy was relaxed for PNG. The men’s national team, the Kumuls, and women’s side, the Orchids, have since played two World Cup games each in Port Moresby.

Advertisement

Other nations, however, have had to stump up as much as $30,000 to the ARL Commission for corporate facilities, a departure from the Pacific Championships where boxes and suites have been supplied to participating countries. “It’s been an absolute joke,” one national official said. The PNG women’s team celebrates scoring a try against France in Port Moresby. Competing nations are also unhappy about the gulf between the treatment of their players and the Australian team. There is a long-standing disparity in player remuneration – members of Kevin Walters’ squad will receive $40,000 for the World Cup while players from other countries will earn only $850 per game. The Australian fees are dictated by the Rugby League Players’ Association’s collective bargaining agreement with the ARL Commission.

Advertisement

But officials at the World Cup are also annoyed at their players having to share twin rooms at rundown hotels and at times sleep in single beds while the Australians are put up in their own rooms at top-end lodgings. V’landys, who has been on a trip to China this week to source equipment for his planned “NRL Land” entertainment centre and meet stadium representatives in Hong Kong, explained the role of the World Cup hosts on Friday. Fiji fans cheer during the Bati’s game against Australia in Brisbane last weekend. Getty Images “Every nation executes a participation agreement. Accordingly, we pay each nation a participation payment,” he said. “In addition, we make payments to the players, pay for flights, accommodation, travel and meals for 32 players and officials [per team]. We also provide 112 complimentary admission tickets [and] prize money of $475,000 each for the men’s and women’s [World Cups]. We invite travelling administrators into [the] official ARLC function.

Advertisement

“As you can see, we cover nearly all costs and pay them to participate. They signed an agreement and knew of the terms. [It’s] disappointing they cherry-pick; as you can see, they receive a very good deal.” V’landys said the pre-tournament complication with PNG emerged because administrators there mistakenly believed they were a host nation and had committed to providing boxes they weren’t entitled to. The Tongan team trains before their blockbuster group game against Samoa at CommBank Stadium on Sunday. Kate Geraghty “We helped them out by giving up the ARLC box and other boxes to cover their mistake,” he said. “We acted in good faith as they made a mistake and were never threatened about them pulling out.” Another source of displeasure among some officials is suggestions that Australia and New Zealand will get first choice of hotels for the semi-finals in Sydney and Newcastle despite the fact the Kiwis will finish second in Pool A in the men’s tournament following a 24-22 defeat to the Kangaroos on October 15.

Advertisement

The reward for winning Pool B, meanwhile, is a six-day turnaround in a secondary hotel in Newcastle. Related Article Exclusive

NRL 2026 This former NRL star was convicted of a horrific stabbing. This is what shocked him in jail National teams are wary about airing their frustrations publicly, considering the importance of Australia to international competition and the comparative commercial might of the ARL Commission, which owns the NRL. However, the experience of this World Cup could shape decision-making regarding the next one. Sources say the International Rugby League will no longer sell rights to the World Cup to a host country or countries and instead plans to run future editions itself, possibly in partnership with the ARL Commission.

Advertisement

Under one scenario to be discussed at an IRL board meeting next week, the ARL Commission would jointly underwrite the 2030 World Cup despite Australia not physically hosting it. The location of the tournament is set to be announced next month. Recent developments have helped convince the international federation, on whose board V’landys sits, to go in the new direction. The IRL is in dispute with England’s Rugby Football League over $800,000 in allegedly outstanding payments from the 2022 World Cup, while the original host of this year’s tournament, France, withdrew for financial reasons, leading Australia to step in.

Wallabies coach Les Kiss has backed veteran Kurtley Beale to compete as an inside centre on the spring tour, opening the door to a potential Test comeback after a five-year absence. Kurtley Beale has been backed by Wallabies coach Les Kiss to compete for a spot as inside centre. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has awarded three ministers additional staffers worth a total of $550,000, as crossbench MPs accuse him of failing to play fair over his power to decide opponents’ staffing levels. Defence Minister Richard Marles, Emergency Management Minister Kristy McBain and Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino each hired an additional staff member between May and October, while allocations for the Greens, One Nation and independents remained flat. Defence Minister Richard Marles (left) and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese (right). Dominic Lorrimer The government now employs 433 adviser-level staff among their 30 ministers, with a maximum total remuneration for the cohort of a little more than $96 million. By comparison, the shadow ministry currently employs 92 advisers on a maximum total remuneration of just above $19 million. The prime minister’s sole discretion to set additional staffing allocations for both his ministers and his opponents has come under increased scrutiny with both One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and independent senator Fatima Payman heaping pressure on Albanese to hand the power to an independent body.

Advertisement

On Thursday, this masthead revealed that One Nation MP David Farley had rejected an unsolicited offer from Albanese to employ an additional staffer, with a $200,000 salary package, over concerns the prime minister was seeking to influence the lower-house politician. It follows similar revelations in this masthead that Albanese wrote a letter guaranteeing 15 staff to the Greens three days before the party teamed up with Labor to reject an inquiry into his power to allocate staff; allowed Senator Tammy Tyrrell to retain additional staff when she joined Labor in May; and offered then-opposition leader Sussan Ley additional staff for support of the government’s attempt to change freedom of information laws. Albanese defended his provision of staffing on Thursday, saying he had increased the staffing allocation to all federal MPs during his time as prime minister. While all federal MPs can now employ five electorate officers, up from four, Albanese has complete discretion over how many higher-paid advisers each MP gets. Electorate officers have a base salary of up to $102,681, while adviser-level staff for ministers can earn up to $317,152, and $167,530 for all other MPs.

The latest data, accurate as of October 1, found Marles and Mulino had each hired one “adviser 3” grade staffer with a base salary up to $167,530. McBain hired an “adviser 2″ grade staffer with a base salary up to $113,521. All three staffers can also collect $35,387 in allowances. Marles now has 20 advisers, McBain has eight and Mulino has seven. Related Article Exclusive

One Nation Albanese offered One Nation MP an extra staffer. Hanson says it’s an attempt at undue influence The offices of Albanese, Marles, Mulino and McBain were all contacted for comment regarding the responsibilities of the additional staff and the specific pay grade determinations. None responded prior to publication. Northern Territory MP Luke Gosling appears to have lost two staffers when he stood aside from a special envoy role after being charged with breaching bail conditions while awaiting a court date for an alleged assault. Gosling’s breach of bail charge has since been dropped. He is facing two charges of assaulting the Northern Territory administrator, which he denies. Payman is the only independent in the parliament who has no advisers. The senator believes Albanese is punishing her for defecting from the Labor Party during the last term of parliament.

Integrity experts and crossbench MPs have repeatedly called for the power to be handed to an independent body over fears the prime minister is “weaponising” his power. MPs’ salaries are set by the independent Remuneration Tribunal, a body that has been floated as a more appropriate way to decide staffing allowances. More than 18,000 passengers boarded driverless trains at stations along the final stage of Sydney’s $30 billion M1 metro line for the first time on Friday morning, creating a carnival atmosphere and ending more than two years of major disruptions. CultureBooksReview Rage, depression, despair: Why is PMDD still so poorly understood? Heidi Maier October 30, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Gender difference is intimately stitched into the fabric of humanity, and at every stage in its long history, medicine has absorbed and enforced socially constructed divisions and assumptions. These divisions have traditionally ascribed power and dominance to men. As modern scientific medicine evolved into a discipline, institution and profession, it flourished within these dynamics. Women were marked by their anatomical difference from men, and medically defined as defective, deficient and deviant. But women also possessed an organ of the highest biological – and social – value: the uterus. Possession of this organ defined the purpose of women: to bear and raise children. Being biologically female defined and constrained what it meant to be a woman. And being a woman was conflated with, and reduced to, “the female sex”. Medicine validated these social determinants by constructing the myth that woman was her biology, both physically and psychologically, and for centuries, women’s illnesses and diseases were consistently related back to the “secrets” and “curiosities” of their reproductive organs, menstruation, pregnancy and childbirth. Writer Laura Elizabeth Woollett.

Advertisement

As much as women’s bodies and their processes have been medicalised and pathologised, so too have female hormonal states tied to menstruation including perimenopause, menopause, premenstrual tension (PMT) and, more recently, the hormonal mental disorder known as premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). Photo: In her first work of non-fiction, Hell Days, Australian novelist Laura Elizabeth Woollett interrogates PMDD, or what she describes as “the inferno of hormonal mood disorder.” Interweaving memoir with investigative journalism and medical research, she explores the condition in several ways: the articulation of her own experience, research into the correlation between the menstrual cycle and mood disturbances, and interviews with fellow sufferers, as well as doctors and research scientists. With the benefit of diagnosis, treatment and hindsight, Woollett writes with clear-eyed honesty about her own jarring, cyclical experiences with PMDD. She remembers, for example, sitting under the harsh fluorescent lighting of the call centre where she worked, actively deciding to avoid taking the train to and from her job because of the depression and suicidal ideation with which she was struggling. She did not, she reveals, trust herself not to jump in front of a train. Likewise, she chronicles many years of emotional (and likely also hormonal) destabilisation, including struggles with mood fluctuations, body image and eating disordered behaviours, that she only correlated with her menstrual cycle while on holiday with her husband in Thailand in 2018. Feelings of heavy depression and vivid death fantasies plagued her until her period came and suddenly, she writes, “I felt fine again.”

Advertisement

She googled “PMS rage depression” and found information about PMDD. It was only then that she became aware of the condition which can cause severe emotional and physical changes before a woman’s period. Symptoms of the disorder can include, but are not limited to, depression, anger, irritability, difficulty concentrating, insomnia, lethargy, feelings of being out of control and suicidality. Most disturbingly, the illness is estimated to affect as many as one in 20 women, one in three of whom will attempt suicide. Related Article Literature Barbara Kingsolver’s hymn to Appalachia and the healing power of art As Woollett’s extensive research and interdisciplinary approach to her topic makes clear, relatively little that is concrete or scientifically verified is known about PMDD. Indeed, it was only in 2013 that the condition was formally moved out of the appendix of the psychiatric bible, the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM), and recognised as a stand-alone depressive diagnostic category. Treatment for the illness remains frustratingly experimental with doctors recommending sufferers take some form of oral contraception, antidepressant medication, hormone replacement therapy or even consider a hysterectomy, and research is predictably underfunded. More needs to be done, clearly, and that urgency underlies the wide-ranging discussions Woollett has with general practitioners, obstetricians and gynaecologists, psychologists and psychiatrists, scientists and researchers, as well as fellow sufferers.

Advertisement

Woollett’s accomplished and deeply impressive book is the second to be published in Australia this year on PMDD and sits comfortably alongside Emma Hardy’s insightful and personal Periodic Bitch as an important exploration of a medical condition that is both affecting vast numbers of women and radically diminishing the quality of their physical and mental health. Ultimately, what both volumes demonstrate is not only the depth and breadth of women and their suffering but that, at the intersection of menstrual and mental health, healthcare providers and broader healthcare systems worldwide are continuing to fail women in their responses to and treatment of their pain. When former jumps jockey Shane Jackson stepped out on his own as a trainer two years ago, he had just four horses in his stable, and 40 boxes to fill. “We had a big empty barn,” Jackson recalled this week. “It was a bit daunting early days.” Trainer Shane Jackson works Victoria Derby hopeful King Snitz in Warrnambool’s Lady Bay. Nicole Cleary Passionate racing identity Tony Ottobre was one of the many owners the Irishman messaged to ask for a horse. Years ago, he had ridden a jumps winner for Ottobre – whose mare Pride Of Jenni is one of Australia’s most popular racehorses – and he was using that as an in. It worked – sort of. Ottobre preferred to send his horses to trainers closer to his home on the peninsula, Jackson was told, and Warrnambool was too far away. Anyhow, he did not have a horse.

Out of the blue about a month later, Jackson said, he received another text from Ottobre, telling the fledgling trainer he had a young colt that was too small to take to the sales. “He had mostly fillies and mares at home and didn’t have the room for him so he said, ‘would you take him and break him in, do what you need to do’,” Jackson said. King Snitz will be trainer Shane Jackson’s first runner in a group 1 race. Nicole Cleary That colt was King Snitz, who on Saturday will be Jackson’s first runner in a group 1 race – in the $3 million Victoria Derby, no less, against the behemoth stables of Ciaron Maher, Chris Waller and Gai Waterhouse. Jackson’s road to the top started in Baltinglass, an Irish town about 60 kilometres south-west of Dublin. A champion claiming jumps jockey in Ireland, their version of an apprentice, Jackson rode in the major festivals at Cheltenham and Aintree.

Advertisement

But the rides dried up during Europe’s economic crisis in the early 2010s, forcing him, his wife Lauren and their young son Joseph to move to Australia in 2012. “The mortgage was getting higher to pay,” Jackson said. “It was either going off to find a different career path or go on an adventure.” They chose the latter. Their initial plan was to stay for three or four years, then make a call. Two more kids later, with another on the way, Jackson and his wife are still here, and dreaming big. Shane Jackson’s King Snitz is one of the leading chances in the Victoria Derby. Nicole Cleary Jackson was among the top hoops in his adopted home. His best seasons came in 2018-19 and 2019-20 when he won back-to-back Tommy Corrigan Medals for the state’s leading jumps jockey. He retired in 2021, aged just 34 and at the top of his game.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

Melbourne Cup Joy for Jamie Melham after late Melbourne Cup scratching: Who’s in the field and who can win His decision was met with surprise, but Jackson wanted to bow out on a high, and free of any life-changing injuries. He was also eager to start the next stage of his racing career. “A lot of sportspeople probably go on for too long, I went out with people wondering why I was giving it away, but I was thinking about training,” Jackson said. Jackson is among the growing number of jumps jockeys aiming to make it as trainers. He’s following in the footsteps of champion trainer Ciaron Maher and rising star Gavin Bedggood, who won this year’s Caulfield Cup with Kingswood. Maher, who started in Warrnambool and for whom he rode a winner, is an inspiration.

Advertisement

“There’s one place these guys want to get and that’s the top,” Jackson said. “If you don’t want to strive to be like that, and you’re happy to rest on your laurels and just be a mediocre trainer – that’s not my goal. “I’d love to on some day be a Ciaron Maher or Chris Waller. We just want to get bigger and get better quality horses and more winners.” Loading The life of a jumps jockey lends itself to becoming a trainer. Often, they do not make enough in prizemoney so need to subsidise their income by working in a stable, giving them a broader understanding of what it takes behind the scenes to get a horse on the track. “It’s not like being a flat jockey, that’s why they reckon jumps jockeys make good trainers in Australia,” Jackson said.

Advertisement

Jackson spent about five years with the former Warrnambool father-son training partnership of Bill and Symon Wilde, “breaking horses on the side” while riding full-time. He has also worked briefly for Darren Weir before his disqualification and in Lindsey Smith’s stables. Though he has held a trainer’s licence since 2022, it was not until 2024 that Jackson went out on his own. Though the challenging early days when he had more empty boxes than horses are gone, his is by no means a major stable. He has about 50 horses on the books, primarily based in Warrnambool with some at Flemington. His staff list has grown to 20. His wife, who works for Bendigo Bank by day, takes care of billing and accounts by night. “We’ve built pretty quick, which is great,” Jackson said. “Just work hard, keep the winners coming so we can keep expanding.” View post on X

King Snitz is the stable star, and Jackson’s first winner at group level after victory in the Norman Robinson Stakes (2000m), a traditional Derby lead-up race. Related Article Updated

Melbourne Cup Leading Melbourne Cup chance ruled out, four runners face a nervous wait Jackson loved the colt from the start. Even from the breaking in process, Jackson could tell King Snitz had a big tank. “[He’s] not the simplest horse to deal with, but you’d never get to the bottom of him when he was at the breaker,” Jackson said. “He was light-framed, small, carrying me around at 70 kg, and you still wouldn’t get him tired. “From day one we liked him. It was a waiting game then to get him to grow and develop and get him to the races.”

Advertisement

The plan this spring was to run King Snitz “two or three” times before tipping him out to the paddock but as his form lifted with the rise in distance, the goals became loftier. “It’s everyone’s dream to win a group 1, no doubt we’ll get there,” Jackson said. “If we could do that in the Derby this Saturday, it’d be amazing. It’d be a wee bit surreal, I suppose, but I think we do have a great chance. “If we can get a group 1 winner knocked off it will definitely help the business and attract better quality horses, and we can feature in these sort of races a bit more often.” Follow our Derby Day live blog from 11am Saturday and stick around for the Melbourne Cup barrier draw on Saturday evening. More than two-thirds of young people are struggling to unwind and feel an increasing sense of uncertainty around the future of artificial intelligence, while cost of living remains the number one concern for Australians aged 18 to 24, according to a new national survey. The annual Gen Z Wellbeing Index, released this week, found that 69 per cent of young Australians feel guilty for relaxing, citing worries around wasting time or feeling that they should be doing something deemed to be productive instead. Two-thirds of Australian Gen Zers said they feel guilty about resting. iStock University student Alyssa Mortimore, 19, said that despite knowing the importance of unwinding, she often felt stressed from doing too much and struggled to take a break. “You’re seeing so many people at times who are overworking themselves to the point where they’re not able to do anything,” she said. “I find I’m still guilty of doing that sometimes as well.”

Advertisement

Despite her peers’ attitudes, Mortimore said taking rest seriously had become something that most helped her adjust to life in Melbourne after moving from the small Tasmanian town of Huonville two years ago. Related Article Opinion

Dating My generation has lost the ability to date in real life. Dating apps aren’t helping Saria Ratnam Student “To go into a big city where your face can practically disappear was very, very jarring,” she said. “It was quite stressful, and I truthfully had a lot of anxiety attacks, which was not enjoyable.” Since then, Mortimore has made hobbies and relaxation – without the expectation of it being productive – a non-negotiable in her schedule. “I really love doing art, especially when I’m not going through the best time mentally,” said Mortimore. “Or if I can’t make art because I’m feeling burnt out, I will just listen to new music.”

Advertisement

Professor of wellbeing science at the University of Melbourne Nikki Rickard said that while experiencing periods of boredom and mental quietness might feel foreign, it is essential for young people’s development and wellbeing. “Mentally, emotionally, even socially – to be able to have time on your own and not depend always on back and forth between other people is a critical part of our natural development,” she said. Dhananjay Nagpal said he uses AI to reassure himself. Jason South Research from the University of Sydney earlier this year found the number of mental disorders in those aged 16 to 24 has surged from 23.4 per cent in 2007 to 36.2 per cent in 2022 – a relative increase of about 54 per cent. Of the survey respondents, one in four (26 per cent) reported they could not manage more than three hours without their phone.

Advertisement

Concerns about the cost of living was ranked as the number one issue for the third year in a row, followed by housing and rental affordability, and mental health. Related Article Opinion

Superannuation House poor, super rich: The one area young Australians are winning Victoria Devine Money columnist The prevalence of AI and concerns about its societal impact was listed as the fourth-most significant concern this year – up from 10th place in 2025. While 34 per cent of participants worried about how AI would impact the future jobs market, one in four Gen Zers turned to AI when in need of life advice. Traditionally, Rickard said, “young people are pretty bad at seeking help for their mental health”, noting that AI technology has helped fill the gaps where stigma or accessibility to services act as a barrier for seeking professional support.

Advertisement

“That’s where AI tools and digital tools offer a level of personalisation that can be really helpful, particularly for marginalised groups,” she said. However, Rickard stressed the importance of using specialised AI tools that have been rigorously trained as professionals are. Dhananjay Nagpal, 20, is studying computer science at the University of Melbourne and said he mostly uses AI for academic purposes, but sometimes to reflect on his own thoughts. “Not asking for advice, but maybe just reassuring myself,” he said. “But again, it’s just a computer, right? So you can’t really trust it.”

Advertisement

University of Melbourne critical thinking researcher Dr Samantha-Kaye Johnston said personalised general-purpose AI systems appeal to young people “because they’re quite convincing in terms of how they anticipate their needs, and they’re available 24/7”. But she warned that in order to be genuinely beneficial to a person’s development, AI chatbots and coaches need to be designed to provide cognitive friction, “which is the intellectual effort that’s involved in questioning information and being comfortable in encountering competing perspectives instead of just immediately receiving an answer”. Johnston said it comes down to encouraging young people to reach a level of autonomy to know when to turn away from chatbots for guidance, and providing them with the skills and tools to know how to turn towards the humans in their lives. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
